item.title: Candidate Once Charged With Murder Loses Bid for Sheriff in Arkansas
item.description:
A candidate for sheriff in Arkansas who shot and killed a man who had been charged with sexually assaulting his 13-year-old daughter lost his bid for office on Tuesday.

The candidate, Aaron Spencer, had won the Republican nomination after being charged with murder in the 2024 fatal shooting of Michael Fosler, 67, who at the time was out on bond while facing a series of felony charges, including sexually assaulting Mr. Spencer’s daughter.

Mr. Spencer, a farmer and contractor, had admitted to shooting the man but pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder, saying he had shot Mr. Fosler while the man had the 13-year-old in his car and was trying to stop her from getting out.

Prosecutors contended that Mr. Spencer had planned the shooting and could have called the police instead.

Mr. Fosler had not entered a plea before he was killed, according to court records.

The murder charge was dropped in June after a judge found that police detectives — ones working for the same office Mr. Spencer ultimately sought to lead — had lost dashboard camera footage that might have captured the shooting and could have aided Mr. Spencer’s defense.

Mr. Spencer captured nearly 45 percent of the vote for sheriff on Tuesday in Lonoke County, Ark., east of Little Rock, but was defeated by Larry Behnke, an independent, according to election officials. About 22,000 votes were cast in the race.

In the earlier primary, Mr. Spencer had ousted the sitting sheriff, who had been in office for more than a decade and whose deputies had arrested Mr. Spencer.

“The voters of Lonoke County have made their decision, and I respect it,” Mr. Spencer wrote on Facebook around midnight.

He asked everyone who supported his candidacy to give Mr. Behnke a “fair shot” and urged those newly involved in local government to continue participating.

“The sheriff answers to you,” he added, “no matter who holds the job.”

Emily Cochrane and Pooja Salhotra contributed reporting.

item.title: Johnson Says He Won’t Seek Re-election for House Leadership
item.description:
Speaker Mike Johnson told Republican aides on Wednesday that he would not run to lead the House G.O.P. conference in the minority, according to a person familiar with the comments, after Democrats’ sweeping takeover of Congress.

The decision paves the way for new Republican leadership in the chamber after the party’s drubbing in the midterm elections. It also caps a stunning arc for Mr. Johnson, who ascended to the most powerful position in the House three years ago after the hard-right faction of his party ousted then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy.

In a letter he sent to G.O.P. lawmakers on Wednesday, Mr. Johnson called serving as speaker “the greatest professional honor of my life” and said that House Republicans during their time in the majority had “defied the odds, proved the skeptics wrong, and accomplished what many thought impossible.” He attributed his decision to wanting to spend more time with his family.

“I love this institution, I love our conference, and I remain as committed as ever to the conservative principles that brought me to Washington,” Mr. Johnson wrote. “But the demands of serving in leadership are immense, and they require sacrifices not only from those entrusted with the responsibility, but also from the families who support them.”

The move did not surprise many on Capitol Hill, given the party’s staggering losses in races across the country. Leaders who preside over such routs are rarely rewarded with stewardship of the party in the minority.

His decision almost immediately touched off what could become a fierce succession battle.

Hours after Mr. Johnson said he would not seek re-election in leadership, his No. 2, Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, sent his own letter to House Republicans announcing his intent to run for minority leader.

“This is no doubt a challenging time for our conference, but overcoming adversity is nothing new to me,” Mr. Scalise wrote. “We will need to be honest with ourselves about what happened, but it is more important now than ever for us to emerge from this stronger and united because the stakes couldn’t be higher.”

Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio, a close ally of President Trump, also jumped in, saying he, too, would seek the top spot. Mr. Jordan, the chairman of the Judiciary Committee, was more pointed in his critique of his party’s current leadership.

“For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us,” Mr. Jordan wrote. “That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democrat majority.”

Both Mr. Jordan and Mr. Scalise vied for the speakership in 2023. But their political battle cost them. Mainstream Republicans blamed Mr. Jordan’s hard-line conservative allies for sabotaging Mr. Scalise’s bid, and they refused to back him. After Mr. Jordan could not secure votes on the floor, his failure cleared the way for Mr. Johnson’s ascent.

item.title: What’s Left? Here Are the Midterm Races That Have Not Been Called.
item.description:
Democrats celebrated a thumping victory after winning large majorities in Congress in the midterm elections on Tuesday. They seized on frustrations over inflation, corporate influence and President Trump. Voters delivered Republicans their biggest losses in decades, unseating them in traditionally conservative states and districts.

But some races were still too close to call Wednesday morning, leaving some questions unanswered: whether Democrats could grow their majorities in the House and Senate, and how far Republicans’ losses would extend.

Here are the races to watch Wednesday:

Mississippi’s Senate seat was too close to call after Scott Colom, a Democratic prosecutor, mounted an unexpectedly competitive challenge against Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican seeking a second full term. He was a mere 43 votes ahead of her early Wednesday, with more than 940,000 ballots counted.

The razor-thin margin contrasts with Mr. Trump’s 23-point lead in Mississippi from 2024. Mr. Colom’s showing comes amid Democratic Senate wins in other solidly Republican states, including Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

Alaska’s Senate race could take longer to be called, as about a quarter of the ballots remained uncounted Wednesday morning. Mary Peltola, the Democrat, had a slight edge in the reported vote over Senator Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, but her lead appeared fragile.

The bulk of the remaining vote was expected to come from mailed ballots in the sprawling state, where ballot deliveries typically take time. It was also unclear whether either candidate would cross the 50-percent threshold needed under Alaska’s election laws to win. If not, the race would go to ranked-choice tabulation, which would not begin until Nov. 18.

Source: A.P. Source: Results and race calls from The Associated Press. County view shows margin of the leading candidate in the votes counted so far.

California’s 22nd District was not called, but Randy Villegas, a progressive Democratic newcomer backed by Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, was leading against Representative David Valadao, a Republican. Democrats’ recent redistricting efforts in the state could buoy their candidates, including in the San Joaquin Valley, which leans more conservative than the rest of the state.

Representative Lauren Boebert, a conservative firebrand backed by Mr. Trump in Colorado’s Fourth District, was slightly behind her Democratic challenger, Eileen Laubacher. About six percent of the votes remained uncounted early Wednesday.

The race in Nevada’s Second District, which encompasses the northern half of the state and has long been seen as deeply conservative, was also leaning toward the Democrat. Teresa Benitez-Thompson was leading against David Flippo, a Republican who was supported by Mr. Trump in an open seat.

In Ohio’s 10th District, which includes Dayton, Representative Mike Turner, a Republican, was behind his Democratic challenger, Kristina Knickerbocker, early Wednesday even though election analysts had rated the race as leaning Republican — another illustration of how far the Democratic wave is headed.

North Carolina’s 14th District had been rated by analysts as likely Republican, but Representative Tim Moore, former speaker of the State House, was trailing his Democratic challenger, Lakesha Womack, early Wednesday.

In New York’s 17th District, north of New York City, the Democrat, Cait Conley, was leading Representative Mike Lawler, a Republican, in a key swing seat early Wednesday. Mr. Lawler conceded on Tuesday, but The New York Times has not made a race call.

Westchester County, part of which makes up a major section of the district, faced widespread issues with voting machines on Tuesday. The counting of the votes was scheduled to resume at 11 a.m., the county board of elections said in a statement early Wednesday.

Michigan’s 10th District, north of Detroit, has trended toward Republicans over the past decade. But Christina Hines, a Democrat, was leading against Michael Bouchard, a Republican, in the fight for the open seat on Wednesday morning.

Michigan’s Seventh District is another purple district that has not been called. Representative Tom Barrett, a Republican seeking another term, was trailing William Lawrence, a progressive Democrat who helped found the Sunrise Movement. The district was the most expensive House race from this cycle, where Republicans outspent Democrats in the total of $66.1 million poured into the district, according to AdImpact.

item.title: Democrats Will Control Most Governorships, a Generational Shift
item.description:
A string of stunning upset victories in governors races across the country will put Democrats in charge of deep-red states where they have not held the top jobs in decades.

Democrats flipped five governors’ seats, all in states that President Trump won in 2024, sometimes by double digits. The victories gave them a total of 29 governorships and control of a majority of American governorships for the first time in a generation.

A race for the Republican-held governor’s seat in Alaska had still not been called by Wednesday morning.

Their wins could expand the state-level resistance to Mr. Trump’s policies on tariffs and immigration, while also putting new Democratic-run states into play as potential swing states in the 2028 presidential election.

Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky, the chairman of the Democratic Governors Association, celebrated the wins as the product of years of work, chiseling away at Republicans’ longtime dominance of governors’ mansions.

“Tonight, we delivered a Democratic governor in every swing state from the past several elections, and we expanded the map,” Mr. Beshear said in an interview on Tuesday. “There will be some 2028 candidates who can compete in a place like Iowa or Ohio.”

Mr. Beshear said the Democrats won with campaigns that were “laser focused on the lives of our people, and not just fealty to Donald Trump.”

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott to become the state’s first Latina governor as well as its first Democratic governor in more than 30 years. She has criticized Mr. Trump’s moves to expand the wall along the U.S.-Mexico border and could become a new opponent to his immigration enforcement efforts in a state with one of the largest Latino populations.

Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, flipped a Republican-held governor’s seat in Georgia, to become the country’s first Black woman governor and Georgia’s first Democratic leader since 2003.

In the Midwest, Amy Acton was elected Ohio’s first Democratic governor in 20 years after a bruising, bitterly personal campaign, and Rob Sand became the first Democrat Iowa has elected since 2006.

Voters in the swing states of Michigan and Wisconsin also elected new Democrats to replace their outgoing Democratic governors.

The race in Kansas to succeed Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat, was still too close to call on Wednesday morning, but the Democratic candidate, State Senator Cindy Holscher, was narrowly leading.

Their wins were a remarkable turnaround from eight years ago, when Democrats held just 16 of the country’s 50 governorships. They steadily gained ground to hold 24 governor’s seats going into the midterm elections.

After Tuesday’s elections, about 75 percent of Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governor, according to the Democratic Governors Association.

No Republicans flipped a Democratic-held governor’s seat this year.

Even in states where Republican governor candidates prevailed, some won by surprisingly slim margins. In Florida, Representative Byron Donalds, a Republican, won the race to succeed Governor Ron DeSantis by fewer than 2 percentage points — a race Republicans won by nearly 20 points four years earlier.

One unlikely bright spot for Republicans was New England. There, Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire and Phil Scott of Vermont — both considered moderate Republicans — easily won re-election.

But nearly everywhere else, Democrats won by tapping into national anger over high prices, the war in Iran and Mr. Trump, in general.

They also tailored their appeals to their state’s specific anxieties.

Mr. Sand, who flipped a governor’s seat in Iowa, focused on cancer rates in farm country. Ms. Lance Bottoms highlighted the erosion of Black voting rights in Georgia. Ms. Hinojosa campaigned on the proliferation of data centers in Texas.

In Nevada, the state’s Democratic attorney general, Aaron Ford, campaigned on worries over a slowdown in Las Vegas’s tourism economy to unseat the incumbent Republican governor, Joe Lombardo.

But fundamentally, they all tapped into a pervasive feeling among voters that Americans’ lives were getting worse and that leaders in Washington and state capitols were not listening.

It is unclear whether the new Democratic governors in Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Georgia will actually be able to do much about that.

Many are expected to face Republican-run state legislatures unlikely to grant Democratic wish lists by undoing abortion bans, raising minimum wages or expanding union protections. Republicans still appeared to have majorities in those state legislatures early on Wednesday, though Democrats in Texas were in a close race to take the Texas House of Representatives.

Still, the Democratic governors will be able to reshape their states by appointing their own agency heads, signing executive orders and vetoing Republican bills they don’t like.

They may also be a new barrier to any Republican efforts to redraw legislative districts ahead of the next presidential election.

item.title: How a Logger From Maine Toppled a Giant of the Senate
item.description:
Troy Jackson was nobody’s first choice to run for the U.S. Senate from Maine. Only weeks before stumbling into one of the most consequential races in the country, he had come in third in the Democratic primary for governor. He looked like a political washout.

But today he is a giant slayer, having toppled a five-term Republican incumbent, Senator Susan Collins, in Tuesday’s election.

How Mr. Jackson, a former logger and state lawmaker from a struggling northern outpost, got from there to here — in just 101 days, no less — is an extraordinary story of the man meeting the moment.

Less than five hours after the polls closed, as he scanned a raucous crowd of supporters chanting his name, he shook his head in apparent disbelief.

“I will be thinking about generations of Mainers who worked in our woods, built our ships, kept our mills running, the people who built this state and deserve a government that works for them,” Mr. Jackson, 58, told a packed hotel ballroom in Portland shortly after midnight. “That is what I am going to fight for every damn day.”

Even amid the blue wave that swept Democrats into power across the country, Mr. Jackson’s triumph over Ms. Collins was notable, considering her seniority in the Senate and five previous statewide wins, versus his abbreviated campaign and limitations as a candidate. A fortuitous mix of personal narrative, message and timing powered him to a victory no one could have imagined just months ago.

Drawing on his working-class roots and populist record as a state senator, Mr. Jackson could empathize with voters’ frustrations and fears like few other congressional candidates. Perhaps even more important, Ms. Collins, despite her efforts to assert her independence, could not escape the shadow of an exceedingly unpopular president — especially in a state hit hard by his tariffs and war with Iran, inflating costs for Mainers dependent on heating oil and trade with their Canadian neighbors.

“It is stars aligning,” said Heather Quinn Cuzzi, a Democratic consultant who has worked in Maine politics for more than 20 years. “It’s the blue wave. It’s the right time. A lot of union folks and working class people have not had a candidate they could be excited about, and Troy gave them a voice.”

Mr. Jackson was an accidental Senate candidate, with no burning desire to go to Washington. But he quickly recalibrated after the implosion of the Democratic Party’s chosen nominee. Graham Platner, an oyster farmer hastily anointed a rising star, was forced to quit the Senate race amid allegations of sexual misconduct. As the possibility of chaos loomed, Mr. Jackson, a card-carrying union member, called in a cavalry of shipbuilders, teachers and mill workers who helped him easily sew up the nomination at a Democratic convention in late July.

Mr. Jackson had less than four months to wipe out Ms. Collins’s 30-year record of constituent services and federal patronage that had brought billions of federal dollars to the state.

“A lot of people were wondering if he was up to the challenge,” said Ethan Strimling, a former state senator and mayor of Portland. “This is the big time, up against one of the all-time pros of Maine history.”

Even before Mr. Jackson sealed the nomination, Maine was rocked by the fatal shooting of a Colombian immigrant by a federal agent in the coastal city of Biddeford. As Mr. Jackson condemned President Trump’s deadly immigration crackdown, the incident helped set the tone for a campaign in which Ms. Collins was repeatedly pressed to defend the administration’s most unpopular policies.

Mr. Jackson lacked Mr. Platner’s rugged charisma and rhetorical skills, and he suffered by comparison — what his senior campaign adviser, David Farmer, called “the Platner hangover.” But at more than 100 public events, including 15 town halls, he endeared himself to voters by sharing stories of his hardscrabble youth in Aroostook County, along the Canadian border. At 19, he followed his father into Maine’s North Woods. At 30, he helped to lead a logging blockade at the border to protest powerful landowners hiring cheaper Canadian labor. Mr. Jackson greeted supporters as “brothers and sisters,” and the labor anthem “Solidarity Forever” became a campaign staple.

“He’s a once-in-a-career candidate for many of us,” said Will Bergeron, a representative of the painters union.

When he wasn’t leaning into his up-from-the-bootstraps biography, Mr. Jackson was pledging to hold the line against a Trump administration he argued was destroying the dreams of the working class. Mr. Jackson, a disciple of Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, pushed a progressive agenda that included doing away with Mr. Trump’s tax cuts, abolishing the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency and establishing a universal health care program. His unflattering portrayal of Ms. Collins as a corrupt creature of Washington was reinforced by a widely circulated ProPublica report that said the F.B.I. had examined her interactions with a donor seeking federal contracts. (Ms. Collins denied any wrongdoing.)

Jia Yang, a 36-year-old restaurant worker who lives in Lewiston, was among the voters who had backed Ms. Collins in the past but said her retirement was overdue.

“I think she’s lost touch with what it means to be an average citizen,” said Mr. Yang, a new father who can tell you the price of diapers and baby formula, even with coupons. “Things are getting worse, and I think we need change.”

Anger over the rising cost of living was a driving force in Senate races across the country. But in Maine, Mr. Jackson also seized on simmering resentment over Ms. Collins’s vote to elevate Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, which cemented the conservative majority that gutted the federal right to abortion.

This race was the first for Ms. Collins, one of the only Republican senators who favor abortion rights, since the demise of Roe v. Wade.

The campaign’s lineup of debates — four in 10 days — posed a major test for Mr. Jackson, a halting and sometimes awkward speaker. He pushed for a town-hall format over traditional debates, but Ms. Collins would not agree, according to Mr. Jackson’s campaign. The matchups ultimately offered few fireworks or gaffes by either candidate until the fourth and final one. “Oh shut up,” Mr. Jackson said to Ms. Collins, after she suggested a heckler “obviously” was his supporter.

Ms. Collins turned the moment into an attack ad that reminded voters about an episode five years earlier when Mr. Jackson was Senate president. During a heated argument with a female lawmaker, he had flung a water bottle, an incident that drew media scrutiny just as he was poised to clinch the nomination. Questions about his temperament surfaced again in campaign’s early days when the Bangor Daily News surfaced a 1988 police report describing his arrest on a charge of misdemeanor assault.

Mr. Jackson apologized for the water-bottle episode. He took responsibility for the fight, which had occurred when he was 19 years old. He did not express regret for his retort during the debate, however.

“What I’m not going to be is talked down to by Senator Collins,” he said in a televised interview. During the debates, she had repeatedly referred to Mr. Jackson, who served as a legislator for nearly 20 years, including six as president of the Maine Senate, as “Troy.”

Her apparent disrespect toward Mr. Jackson permeated the race — and may have backfired. A Republican super PAC denigrated Mr. Jackson’s longtime partnership with Lana Pelletier, his second cousin, in an ad that included a crude jingle. Ms. Collins called for the spot to come down but weeks earlier, she had arguably laid the groundwork by taking a swipe at Mr. Jackson’s relationship. “I never imagined U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and her allies would stoop this low,” Ms. Pelletier, who has two sons with Mr. Jackson, wrote in a column responding to the attacks.

Ms. Collins also ran a widely criticized ad in the homestretch of the campaign featuring a supporter who scoffed, “We’re not talking about buying a cord of wood here. We’re sending someone to the U.S. Senate, and Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective.”

Ms. Collins and her allies outspent the Democrats by about $40 million, according to AdImpact, with a deluge of attack ads that decried Mr. Jackson as a “crook” and a “creep.” Voters at town hall meetings urged Mr. Jackson to fight back more aggressively.

“In general, he allowed those things to roll off his back,” said Charles Dingman, chairman of the Maine Democratic Party. “Or he greeted them with humor.”

For Halloween, Mr. Jackson dressed up as a cord of wood. Three days before the election, he was already having the last laugh.

Tim Balk contributed reporting from Maine.

item.title: Vance, in Break With Trump, Blames Iran War for Republicans’ Rout
item.description:
Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday placed the blame for Republicans’ wipeout in the midterm elections squarely on the war with Iran, in a remarkable break from President Trump’s defense of his decision to attack.

In a more than 600-word post on social media, Mr. Vance also offered a broader critique of the Trump administration’s agenda and messaging in what appeared to be an effort to separate himself from the president.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Mr. Vance wrote. “The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”

In fact, Mr. Trump told The New York Times on Tuesday night that he had no regrets about the war, though he acknowledged voters “weren’t happy with the oil price.”

“That’s a decision that was a very wise decision for the future of the country and the world,” he said.

Since he became Mr. Trump’s running mate, Mr. Vance had been widely seen as the front-runner to succeed the president and inherit the mantle of the Make America Great Again movement Mr. Trump started. But after Tuesday’s disastrous results, Republicans are already rethinking what the future of the party looks like, and Mr. Vance’s post suggests he is willing to separate himself from Mr. Trump as he considers his own political future.

And yet, the post was not a complete break from Mr. Trump. Before Mr. Vance posted the message, he shared it with the president and received positive feedback, one person briefed on the matter said.

Mr. Trump also told reporters Wednesday afternoon that Mr. Vance’s assessment was “largely true.”

“If I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again,” he said, saying he had “no choice” but to attack Iran.

And Mr. Trump speculated about whether Mr. Vance would go ahead with a presidential bid.

“Maybe he won’t run,” he said. “I don’t know who’s going to run.”

Before Tuesday, Mr. Vance’s allies said that the vice president was in no rush to make a decision about running for president, and that he was unlikely to do so until next year.

In his post on social media, Mr. Vance said that many of the voters who supported him and Mr. Trump showed up in the elections, but that they chose to elect Democrats. He said a Republican pollster he called “one of the smartest people I know in politics” identified the four main reasons voters abandoned Republicans: They wanted to end the war, focus on inflation, put America first and change the country’s relationship with Israel.

That implicitly put Mr. Vance at odds with Mr. Trump, who has steadfastly defended the war with Iran, dismissed affordability concerns as a “hoax” and has closely aligned himself with Israel and its leader, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

“Everyone knows why we lost,” Mr. Vance wrote. “And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

item.title: Georgia Governor Nixes Rushed Redistricting Before G.O.P. Loses Power
item.description:
Gov. Brian Kemp of Georgia shut down speculation on Wednesday that he would call a special legislative session to rush through new congressional maps favorable to Republicans or weaken the powers of his office before his Democratic successor, Keisha Lance Bottoms, could assume it.

“The voters of our state have spoken,” Mr. Kemp, a two-term Republican incumbent leaving office because of term limits, said in a statement on Wednesday morning. “As long as I’m governor, we will always respect the results of secure, accessible, and fair elections, and also abide by the laws and constitution of our state.”

A Supreme Court decision that weakened the Voting Rights Act has prompted Republican lawmakers across the South to redraw federal and state legislative boundaries to benefit their party, eliminating districts that had been created to promote minority representation.

Georgia’s legislature had resisted doing that, despite calls from President Trump and some Republicans in the state to take action. Mr. Kemp declined to redraw maps before the midterm elections, noting that early voting in the primaries had, by that point, already started.

He then called a special session in June to draw up new maps for the 2028 election. But less than an hour after the session began, Republican legislative leaders came out and said they would not present new maps after all.

They cited a desire for a methodical process that would include greater input from voters, rather than rushing legislation through, but the decision was also a recognition of mounting protests against redistricting and fears that moving forward could undermine their party’s already enfeebled fortunes in the midterm elections.

There was also an implicit expectation among many political observers that the matter had been shelved only temporarily, and that a narrow window between the election and when a new governor takes power would provide an opportunity not only to enact new maps but also to strip away some of the authority of the governor’s office. The chatter intensified as polls indicated a greater possibility of victory for Ms. Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta and the first Democrat to be elected governor of Georgia in more than 25 years.

Mr. Kemp moved immediately to cut off that possibility, but he said there were “budgetary issues that may need to be addressed before the convening of the regular session in January.”

item.title: With Democrats’ Sweep, Congress Is Set to Reassert Power to Check Trump
item.description:
The Democratic sweep of the House and Senate that has upended the balance of power in Washington has also given an atrophied Congress an opportunity to reclaim its relevance and constitutional role as a check on the president after two years of Republican compliance.

Since President Trump was elected in 2024 along with G.O.P. House and Senate majorities, Republicans on Capitol Hill have defined their role mainly as empowering him and beating back Democratic resistance. That has allowed the executive branch to act with near impunity, steamrolling Congress on spending, tariffs and war powers.

Now, with Democrats set to take firm control of both chambers in a rebuke to Mr. Trump and the Republicans who ceded much of their power to him, the legislative branch is poised to reassert itself in multiple ways — notably on spending and oversight. Democrats say they are determined to investigate and push back against the president and his administration.

“We are going to bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption on this country,” said Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat who is in line to become speaker.

On Wednesday in Washington, as the scope of Democratic victories came into sharper focus, he declared, “The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over.”

Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, also vowed that Democrats would bring about the an end of an era: “The days of Trump’s supplicant Senate are over,” he said.

Despite their aggressive intentions and the scope of their electoral victories, Democrats may be limited in their ability to restrain the president. Mr. Trump has demonstrated a disregard for the power of Congress and the traditional norms that govern the relationship between the legislative and executive branches.

Mr. Trump told Fox News before the elections that he intended to be “Mr. Veto” if Democrats seized control. But as the results — and the obvious backlash — poured in from across the nation, the president struck a more conciliatory tone, saying he would be willing to cut some deals.

It was reminiscent of his first term, when the president, embracing his art-of-the-deal persona, seemed open to bargaining with Democrats on big issues. But partisanship has hardened considerably since then, and Democrats, bolstered by the reach of their victory, are going to press for any deals to be made more on their terms than his.

It is also likely that the administration will put up fierce resistance to attempts by Democrats in Congress to demand answers from executive branch officials, which could spark major conflict and poison efforts to work together legislatively.

In their appearances before Congress over the past two years, Trump administration officials have been dismissive and confrontational with minority Democrats sitting on panels run by friendly Republicans. Democrats will wield those gavels beginning in January, with the accompanying subpoena power to pursue what they see as a target-rich environment of activities and people that merit thorough investigation. Senate Democrats will also have veto power of their own and will be able to delay or block confirmation of Mr. Trump’s judicial and executive branch nominees if they choose.

Top Democrats say they hope the election defeat attributed in many respects to the president will persuade more Republicans to break with Mr. Trump — even at the risk of angering the now weakened president — and join them in pushing back against the White House and even undoing some of its actions.

But Senator John Thune, the South Dakota Republican and current majority leader, took a combative stance as the losses piled up Tuesday night, saying Republicans would not let “fringe” Democratic positions become mainstream. Even with their gains, Democrats remain short of the 60 votes needed to overcome the filibuster, allowing Republicans to retain some leverage.

“Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done,” Mr. Thune said. “Thankfully, we still have President Trump in the White House, and we’ll work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism.”

Democrats say they intend to give Republicans the chance to show whether they took any lessons away from the drubbing by forcing votes on reversing cuts to health care and other safety net programs that hurt rural areas where voters rejected Republicans.

“We are going to challenge them,” Mr. Schumer said. “We are going to put some easy things on the floor and see if they vote for them.”

Democrats will have some challenges of their own. Their members have sharp ideological differences that could be difficult to bridge, lessening the party’s ability to reach consensus. And despite Mr. Trump’s sudden impulse to cut bargains, legislative agreements could be hard to come by, frustrating voters who demanded sudden change.

Spending fights could be particularly thorny. Democrats will want to reclaim congressional spending authority after Republicans used a special party-line process to fund Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown after Democrats balked, leading to an extended shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security.

The administration also refused to spend some money Congress had allocated and shifted other money to pay for Mr. Trump’s pet projects in ways lawmakers have not approved. The administration has also applied its “rescission” authority to strip out money in a way that lawmakers in both parties say breaks budget laws.

Democrats will be eager to restore Congress’s spending prerogatives and could look for help from some Republicans on the House and Senate Appropriations Committees who were quietly unhappy with the president’s spending decisions.

The congressional obeisance to Mr. Trump was clearly a factor in the election outcome, as Democratic candidates skewered Republicans on Capitol Hill for standing on the sidelines while Mr. Trump neutered them and took actions detrimental to their states and districts.

“We’ve got a Republican senator, Roger Marshall, who in essence is a ‘yes man’ to the president,” Adam Hamilton, the Democrat who defeated Mr. Marshall in Kansas, said on MS NOW. “Instead of fighting for the people of Kansas, he comes back as though he’s a spokesperson for the White House.”

In his remarks after the results, Mr. Jeffries said the outcome was the beginning of the “great American comeback.” It could be a comeback for Congress as well.

item.title: ‘They Got Mauled’: How Trump’s Audacious Redistricting Push Backfired
item.description:
Starting last summer, President Trump pushed Republicans to engage in an extraordinary mid-decade redistricting project to overhaul congressional maps in favor of the G.O.P. The goal was to protect a House majority during his final two years in office.

It did not work.

Instead, Democrats on Tuesday gained at least eight seats in Republican-run states that had redistricted over the past 16 months. It was a stiff rebuff for a plan to sort just enough Republicans into just enough districts to give the party a 20-seat House firewall.

Months of political warfare, including more than $200 million in spending on referendums in California and Virginia, simply did not anticipate an electorate that backed House Democratic candidates by 13 percentage points.

No map could have produced a Republican advantage strong enough to withstand such a Democratic wave.

“Donald Trump and Republicans poked the bear, and they got mauled,” said John Bisognano, president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee. “There’s no way to look at this cycle and not see that the scheme to gerrymander the country was a complete and utter catastrophe.”

The plan’s demise illustrated once again the perpetual elasticity of the American electorate. Just as the coalitions that elected Barack Obama president in 2008 had evaporated by 2010, groups that backed Mr. Trump in 2024 abandoned him for 2026.

On Wednesday, House Democratic leaders crowed about defeating the Republican redistricting. They stood in front of a poster featuring a May social media post from James Blair, who ran Mr. Trump’s political operation, in which he boasted that redistricting would net the G.O.P. 16 seats.

“The American people hate it when politicians try to pick their voters,” said Representative Suzan DelBene of Washington State, who leads the House Democrats’ campaign arm.

It will take weeks and precinct-level analysis of election results to determine whether Republicans would have won more seats had they not redistricted at all. But Adam Kincaid, the executive director of the National Republican Redistricting Trust, said on Wednesday that without redrawn maps, his party likely would have lost five more House seats than it did.

He also said Democrats likely cost themselves two House seats in California that they could have won with the 2024 map.

Perhaps nowhere better demonstrated the futility of the Republicans’ plans than Texas and North Carolina. Texas Republicans anticipated that the Hispanic swing toward Mr. Trump in 2024 would be durable. Instead, five districts in Hispanic-heavy South Texas moved to Democrats.

North Carolina legislators redrew congressional lines ahead of both the 2024 and 2026 elections, producing a map intended to deliver 11 of the state’s 14 districts to Republicans. Though not all of Tuesday’s races have been called, Democrats appear on pace to win 10 out of the 14 seats.

In Florida, Republicans gained zero seats in a map they believed would give them four held by Democrats. An Ohio map designed to shift two seats to Republicans may have handed two more to Democrats. And new maps drawn to squeeze out Democrats in Alabama and Tennessee also failed.

At the same time, Democrats are poised to gain several seats from new California congressional districts they drew in response to the Republican effort. There also will be a new Democratic congressman in Utah, where judges ordered new maps. And White House attempts to force new districts were foiled by legislators in Indiana and Nebraska and the courts in Missouri.

It could have been worse for Republicans. The Virginia Supreme Court invalidated a voter-approved plan that likely would have handed 10 of the state’s 11 congressional seats to Democrats. Under the existing map, Democrats are likely to win eight.

The redistricting fight is likely not over. Democrats on Tuesday won control of state governments in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, which could redraw maps to secure seats for their party.

Maryland voters approved a referendum to allow legislators to draw the state’s one Republican House district out of existence. And Republicans may still attempt new maps in South Carolina and Mississippi.

Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas, who lost his bid for a fourth term, could call a special session before the year’s end and ask legislators for yet another new map that could help Republicans recoup their losses.

In Georgia, however, Gov. Brian Kemp said Wednesday morning that he would not call a special session to redistrict before he hands over control to Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms.

item.title: On the Democrats’ Agenda: Investigations of Trump and His Family
item.description:
A $1.4 billion cryptocurrency windfall. Well-timed stock trades. A wedding after-party bankrolled by a Kremlin-connected businessman.

For nearly two years, congressional Democrats were powerless to probe these potential scandals and conflicts looming over President Trump and his family businesses. But after pulling off a landslide midterm election victory that amounted to a sweeping rebuke of the president, they will soon seize control of Congress — and with it, the power to open investigations, hold hearings and issue subpoenas.

Representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat poised to chair the House Oversight Committee, summed up the threat succinctly in a statement late Tuesday: “Lawyer up.”

In an interview on Wednesday, Mr. Garcia said that his warning was meant chiefly for people at the White House who “engaged in corruption” and enriched themselves. “The Trump crime family is the top of our investigative priorities,” he said.

Subpoenas, though, do not guarantee a fruitful investigation.

Some of the president’s business associates and allies are expected to fight some of the subpoenas in court, which could become a lengthy process. And even if the Democrats shed new light on moneymaking ventures, there is no indication that the Trump family violated the law — potentially complicating any effort to pursue impeachment proceedings against the president.

Still, Mr. Garcia and other congressional leaders believe they will find a target-rich environment.

After winning back the White House two years ago, Mr. Trump abandoned his first-term pledge to rein in his family’s deal making, enabling new ventures that enriched the president, his sons and some of his advisers. He shrugged off concerns about conflicts of interest, contending that he “found out that nobody cared.”

He turned out to be wrong. An AP exit poll found that government corruption was a crucial issue for many voters, and that roughly seven in 10 voters said Congress was doing “not enough” to provide checks and balances on the presidency.

In the House, the Oversight and Judiciary committees will lead the investigative efforts, which will not be limited to the Trump family business. Senator Maggie Hassan, the New Hampshire Democrat in line to chair the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, is expected to conduct her own investigations as well.

“We need to zero in quickly on the forms of systemic pay-to-play corruption that are destroying the rule of law and have cost the public huge amounts of money,” Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat expected to lead the House Judiciary Committee, said in a statement.

Here are some of the main issues that Democrats are expected to investigate.

Mr. Trump’s financial returns have multiplied during his second term, largely thanks to his crypto businesses. Those ventures pulled in at least $1.4 billion in revenue last year, a windfall that posed unparalleled potential conflicts of interest.

Congressional investigators will most likely focus on the Trump family’s main crypto company, World Liberty Financial. Last year, an investment firm tied to the United Arab Emirates bought a huge stake in World Liberty. Four months later, the Emiratis struck a deal with the Trump administration — over the objections of some national security officials — for the export of valuable computer chips.

Mr. Trump also collected hundreds of millions of dollars from sales of his $TRUMP memecoin, a type of cryptocurrency that is typically treated like a collectible, and World Liberty’s sale of its own digital tokens. The buyers included foreign entities and businesses seeking relief from the Trump administration.

The activities of the president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., are another top priority for Democrats.

Mr. Trump Jr. has not made things easy for himself. He allowed a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars to help finance his wedding after-party in the Bahamas this year, drawing outrage from congressional Democrats. The president has said that his son repaid the businessman, Umar Kremlev, but Mr. Garcia has flagged it as an investigative target.

Mr. Raskin has also begun investigating 1789 Capital, a venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a senior partner. Several of the companies that 1789 has invested in have received government funding while others benefited from Trump policies.

In a statement, a spokesman for Donald Trump Jr. said that he “is a private citizen who holds no position in government and has broken no laws.”

The statement added that Mr. Trump Jr. “has never sought to influence government policy or official decision making for the benefit of his personal business interests and has every right to pursue lawful and legitimate business and investment opportunities.”

Jared Kushner, a son-in-law of the president, is also on the Democrats’ radar.

Mr. Kushner is not a formal member of Mr. Trump’s government, but he has operated as a top envoy in negotiations to resolve President Trump’s war with Iran and Russia’s war in Ukraine. Mr. Raskin has called for Mr. Kushner to recuse himself from those negotiations, partly citing potential conflicts arising from Mr. Kushner’s private equity firm, Affinity Partners, which has received investments from foreign nations that have a stake in those conflicts.

“Partisan politics aside, no one has ever pointed to a specific legal or ethical guideline that Jared or Affinity has violated,” Chad Mizelle, an attorney for Mr. Kushner, said in a statement on Wednesday.

Unlike his first term, when the Trump family real estate business swore off all new foreign deals, the president imposed few restrictions on deal-making in his second term. That omission opened the door for the Trump Organization to announce new international property deals in Qatar and Saudi Arabia, among others, licensing the family name in exchange for payments.

There is no indication that the Trump Organization linked these deals to foreign policy. And although real estate projects are potentially lucrative for the company, they represent a small fraction of what the president earned last year, meaning they will likely draw less scrutiny.

In the first three months of this year, President Trump’s brokerage accounts placed more than 3,600 trades, and some of those trades appeared to be well timed.

In February, nine days after Mr. Trump’s account executed a purchase of more than $1 million in Dell stock, the president praised the company and its founder, Michael Dell, at an event in Georgia. The Pentagon later announced a $9.7 billion contract with Dell.

There is no indication that the contract was related to the president’s stake in the company, and the trade represented a small fraction of his overall investment portfolio. The Trump Organization has said that the president and his family have no ability to direct the trading, all of which is controlled by outside brokerage firms.

Democrats nonetheless seized on the timing. Senator Elizabeth Warren, the Massachusetts Democrat in line to lead the banking committee, has previously pushed for an investigation into Mr. Trump’s trades.

Democrats might also examine the protection Mr. Trump’s own administration provided him from Internal Revenue Service scrutiny.

In a stunning order this spring, then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche told the I.R.S. to halt any ongoing investigations into Mr. Trump, two of his sons and their businesses. Mr. Blanche’s order also barred the I.R.S. from starting any new audits of the tax returns that the Trumps had, at that point, already filed.

Historically, the I.R.S. has audited the sitting president’s tax returns every year, as a way to signal that even the occupant of the Oval Office has to comply with the nation’s tax laws.

A congressional investigation would most likely focus on the circumstances and legality of the Justice Department granting Mr. Trump this protection, which came after Mr. Trump sued the I.R.S. over the leak of his tax returns.

The Trump family is hardly the only area of interest.

Democrats made it clear during the campaign that they planned to use their newfound congressional oversight powers to look at corruption allegations across the Trump administration.

Mr. Garcia has said he plans to investigate “corporate corruption,” including looking at whether donors to projects such as the White House ballroom may have leveraged their contributions to benefit from Trump administration decisions or government contracts.

He also plans to continue the House’s investigation into the government’s handling of its criminal case against Mr. Epstein, who died in prison in 2019, and his potential links to Mr. Trump. Mr. Garcia has pushed to subpoena Mr. Blanche, who oversaw the release of the Epstein files, a move that Republicans have resisted.

Mr. Raskin also has vowed to investigate the lucrative pardon industry that has sprung up around the Trump administration.

Ms. Hassan said she planned to investigate the Trump administration’s use of no-bid contracts to donors and other allies of the president. Several deals, including a lucrative contract for deportation planes that was approved under Kristi Noem’s tenure as homeland security secretary, have come under intense scrutiny.

House lawmakers plan to scrutinize top officials involved in the administration’s immigration agenda, including Stephen Miller, a top White House aide; Tom Homan, Mr. Trump’s border czar; and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, according to a person with knowledge of the discussions.

In both the House and Senate, Democrats will also seek to use their subpoena power to investigate the killings of Americans by federal immigration officers, including two shootings in Minneapolis at the beginning of the year.

As they sought to make the war in Iran a focus of their campaigns, Democrats also signaled plans to investigate Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who is already facing an impeachment effort.

So far, Democratic leaders have demurred when discussing an impeachment effort against the president, with many lawmakers wary after their two efforts to remove him from office in his first term came up short.

Madeleine Ngo and Zolan Kanno-Youngs contributed reporting

item.title: Why Doesn’t Mississippi Allow Election Recounts?
item.description:
An unusual situation is brewing in Mississippi, the only state in the country with no legal provision that allows for a recount of votes in a statewide election.

The Democratic candidate for Senate, Scott Colom, leads the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, by 65 votes as of Wednesday afternoon — an incredibly tight race that would trigger an automatic recount in dozens of other states.

In fact, 47 states have a provision for an automatic recount if a contest is close or if a candidate requests a recount. Two more states, Illinois and Tennessee, allow recounts if a candidate mounts a formal legal challenge.

Most state recount provisions were instituted during the last century as a result of legal challenges that made their way to state supreme courts. But Mississippi has no recount law on the books, leaving it unprepared to handle a particularly close election.

There are still small batches of ballots to be counted in the state, and the margin between the candidates may widen. Mississippi, unlike many states, accepts mail-in ballots that arrive five days after Election Day, drawing out the counting process.

Ultimately, however, there is no legal path to a recount in the state. Derek Muller, a professor and expert on election law at the University of Notre Dame, said that a losing candidate could instead pursue a legal challenge over the inclusion of specific ballots or sets of ballots, which could result in a change in vote totals.

item.title: Helicopter Crash Off Miami Kills One Person and Injures Two
item.description:
A man was killed and two others were injured on Wednesday morning after the helicopter they were traveling in crashed in Biscayne Bay off Miami, the authorities said.

A Robinson R44 helicopter fell into the water around 11:15 a.m. local time, the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement. The U.S. Coast Guard in Miami said one person on board had been killed.

Two other men were injured when the helicopter went down near Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park at the southern tip of the village of Key Biscayne, about seven miles from downtown Miami, according to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, which responded to the scene with other agencies.

The injured men were transported to a hospital and were in critical but stable condition, Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz of the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said at a news conference. Their identities were not released.

Sheriff Cordero-Stutz said the helicopter had been chartered and was filming boats in the water when the crash happened. She said she did not know the name of the company operating the helicopter or what airport it had departed from.

Video from NBC6, a local television station, showed the aircraft apparently upside down in the water and surrounded by yellow floats on the surface. The helicopter remained underwater late Wednesday afternoon.

It was not clear what caused the crash and where the helicopter had been heading.

The F.A.A. said it was investigating the episode with the National Transportation Safety Board. The Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said it was investigating as well.

item.title: The Democratic Wave Swept State Houses Across the Country
item.description:
The Democratic surge on Tuesday netted at least 330 state legislative seats, from New Hampshire to Arizona, giving the Democrats full control of 22 state governments and making them the majority in a dozen statehouse chambers where they had been the minority party.

And while Washington remains divided, Democrats will have the power to make policy on health care, voting and taxation in state capitals that for years have been far beyond their control, such as Texas, Georgia and North Carolina.

In Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Nevada, Democrats will hold both statehouse chambers as well as the governorship. The party was on the verge of the same “trifecta” in Arizona as well.

“Our victories have shattered Republicans’ grip on our statehouses,” said Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee.

The victories in state legislative races rarely grab national headlines, but statehouses exert enormous influence on issues that directly affect day-to-day life, from health care coverage to transportation. Some of those wins were the fruits of long rebuilding efforts. In Wisconsin, the fight to dismantle a Republican gerrymander of legislative districts finally delivered the Democrats both the State Senate and House, while the party retained the governor's mansion in Madison.

Elsewhere, state-level victories were almost incidental consequences of a wave that was bigger than even the most optimistic Democrat has anticipated.

The Arizona Senate’s minority leader, Priya Sundareshan, went to sleep Tuesday night with a statement saying she looks forward to seeing the votes counted. By morning, it was clear the changes would be huge.

“I’m really excited to be in the driver’s seat,” Ms. Sundareshan said.

Even in several states where Democrats did not win a majority, they still won enough seats to prevent Republican supermajorities, which confer the ability to override a governor’s veto.

Most notable were Iowa, where Rob Sand, a Democrat, won the governor’s race, and Ohio, where, Amy Acton, also a Democrat, was elected governor. They are their states’ first Democratic governors in 16 years, and with no Republican supermajority, both will have more leverage than they would otherwise have had.

State legislators allocate billions of dollars for schools, prisons and health care, and can shape policies on everything from data centers to taxes before Congress does. In Wisconsin, one of 10 states that have not expanded Medicaid access under the Affordable Care Act, Democrats now have the power to do so. But even in Texas and Georgia, the new Democratic governor and the one Democratic chamber will almost certainly apply enormous pressure to expand Medicaid as citizens struggle with health care costs.

And while legislative elections are typically overshadowed by midterm races for governor and Congress, this year’s races did command more attention — and money, including $100 million from the States Project, a Democratic group — in part because of the frenzied mid-decade U.S. House redistricting. Now the question of redistricting moves to the 2028 election, and the prospect of redrawing even more congressional maps, this time by Democrats.

The weakening of the Voting Rights Act by the Supreme Court in April had raised the prospects of states such as Texas and Georgia taking up redistricting again with an eye on diluting Democratic districts drawn to give Black and Hispanic voters more power. Now that those states have divided governments, a Republican redistricting would be impossible.

But Wisconsin and Pennsylvania could turn the tables on Republicans if their Democratic leaders choose to.

The earliest tally of state legislative results has Democrats netting at least 330 statehouse seats, but the number is sure to climb, perhaps as high as 800 seats. There is little doubt they will outperform 2018, when they gained more than 300 during Mr. Trump’s first term.

It was likely the best Democratic result since they gained more than 600 seats in 1974, right after Watergate, said Katy Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting for the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Republicans gingerly pointed to President Trump’s abysmal approval ratings and the same headwinds of inflation, war and fuel costs that cost them the U.S. House and Senate, but also to governor’s races that went badly for the G.O.P.

“The national political environment and the impact of top-of-the-ticket races significantly affected our candidates’ ability to defy historical trends,” Edith Jorge-Tuñón, president of the Republican State Leadership Committee, said in a statement.

It remains to be seen whether the final tally will be as seismic as 2010, when Republicans unleashed their Redistricting Majority Project, or Redmap, and flipped 22 chambers and more than 700 seats — a “shellacking,” as former President Barack Obama described it.

That pendulum swing enabled Republicans to redraw maps and over the next decade to enact conservative policies to weaken labor unions, cut taxes, restrict voter access and expand education vouchers.

The president’s party has lost statehouse seats in 20 of the last 22 midterms, so Tuesday’s results were hardly a surprise, though a year ago the Republican State Leadership Committee held out hope for gains in Michigan, Minnesota and Pennsylvania. Insead, all three of those statehouses will be completely in Democratic hands all with Democratic governors.

Democrats have done well in special elections to fill state legislative seats, but Democratic voters historically have chosen candidates at the top of the ticket, while leaving down- ballot races blank. That was not the case, however, on Tuesday.

And on a night full of unexpected results, one standout was North Carolina. Only three years ago, Democratic legislators were in a superminority, after State Representative Tricia Cotham, a Democrat, switched parties and gave Republicans the power to override former Gov. Roy Cooper’s veto and enact the state’s most restrictive abortion policy in 50 years.

After the Democrats broke that North Carolina supermajority in 2024, their goal for this year’s midterms was simply to chip away at the Republican majority in one of the country’s most gerrymandered states.

Instead, bolstered by Mr. Cooper’s resounding victory for U.S. Senate, they seized control of the House and narrowed the gap in the Senate, bolstering Mr. Cooper’s Democratic successor, Gov. Josh Stein. Ms. Cotham lost her seat.

A similar dynamic unfolded in Georgia and Texas, where Democrats won both states’ Houses of the Representatives for the first time since the early 2000s, as part of a sweep of all statewide races, as well as the governorships

History was also on the verge of being made in Arizona, as Democrats appeared poised to claim both the House and Senate, as one of six new trifectas. Arizona Democrats have not had an outright majority in any chamber since the early 1990s, and not had full control since the mid-1960s.

And though Gov. Phil Scott of Vermont, a popular moderate Republican, won a record sixth term, statehouse Democrats regained the supermajority they had lost in 2024.

Victories by Mr. Scott and Gov. Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were among the few bright spots for Republicans. They also held firm in conservative strongholds like Wyoming, Montana, Idaho and the Dakotas.

Still, there were cracks in Republican redoubts. In Missouri, Democrats broke the supermajority in both the House and Senate. And in Arkansas, Democrats gained a projected 10 seats in the State House.

Last week, Jay Morgan, a former chairman of the Georgia Republican Party, said the national outlook looked dire.

“There’s the potential of a total washout,” he said. “There are seats in play that nobody thought would be in play.”

He was proved right.

Sejal Govindarao contributed reporting.

item.title: Texas Democrats Prepare to Relearn a Skill: How to Govern
item.description:
For Texas Democrats, the hits just keep on coming.

After routing Republicans in every statewide race and overturning a generation of conservative, one-party rule, the Democrats have also taken control of the Texas House of Representatives. The last time they held the majority in either legislative chamber was 2003.

Republicans will keep their majority in the Texas Senate. But the lieutenant governor, who, as the president of that chamber, is arguably the single most powerful force in lawmaking, will also be a Democrat: Vikki Goodwin. So is the governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa.

For the first time in about 25 years, Texas Democrats will have a real chance to govern. “Democrats have to deliver,” Gene Wu, the chairman of the Texas House Democratic Caucus, said from his home in Houston on Wednesday morning. “No excuses, no whining, no crying.”

Mr. Wu was wasting no time. He planned to drive to the state capital, Austin, on Wednesday to prepare for the next legislative session in January.

The Texas Legislature meets only once every two years, making the pressure especially high on Democrats to deliver real policymaking wins — and quickly. They’ve promised to focus their attention on pocketbook issues like taxes and education funding.

For a dozen years, Republicans forced Texas further to the right. Conservative legislators outlawed abortion, banned diversity offices in colleges, legalized the open carrying of firearms on their campuses, and stripped rights from the state’s gay community. They targeted big cities, all run by Democrats, by restricting local control.

Gov. Greg Abbott and Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick led those efforts. Both men lost their re-election bids.

Mr. Wu said his party’s wins were a rebuke to big government policies that he said have come to define the modern Republican Party.

“We’re going to let cities decide if they want to have rainbow sidewalks again,” Mr. Wu said, referencing recent Republican-enforced bans on such displays.

Senfronia Thompson, a Houston Democrat first elected before women could easily have credit cards, is the early favorite for House speaker. She would be the first Black Texan and the first woman in the role.

Tom Oliverson, the chairman of the House Republican Caucus, said the future for his party looked brighter than the present.

“When you kind of hit the bottom,” he said, “you can only go up from there, right?”

item.title: Medical Professionals Are Among the Winners of the Midterms
item.description:
About a half-dozen Democrats who flipped Republican congressional seats are doctors and nurses, many of whom made health policy and their opposition to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s agenda central to their campaigns.

Senator-elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina, a pediatrician, repeatedly called out Mr. Kennedy as her “archnemesis.” She and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan appear to be the first Democratic doctors elected to the Senate in about 60 years.

In California, Representative-elect Richard Pan, a pediatrician and a former state legislator who worked to tighten vaccine exemptions, beat the incumbent, Kevin Kiley, a former Republican who this year ran as an independent.

“This election cycle, R.F.K. Jr. was hands down our No. 1 recruitment and fund-raising tool,” said Erik Polyak, executive director of 314 Action, an organization that spent $30 million to support Democratic scientists and health care professionals.

Other successful health care candidates who flipped House districts include Kristina Knickerbocker, an oncology nurse practitioner in Ohio, and Mitchell Berman, a former Veterans Affairs nurse in Wisconsin. Amish Shah, an emergency room physician, appears to be on track to win in a competitive Arizona district, and Adam Hamawy, a plastic surgeon, won a safe Democratic seat in New Jersey.

Their success reflects, in part, the overall momentum of Democrats in Tuesday’s election. “It was a good thing to be a Democrat last night,” said Kristoffer Shields, director of the Eagleton Science and Politics Program at Rutgers-New Brunswick. Still, they ran, at least in part, on their credibility as medical professionals, “and it clearly seems to have worked,” he said.

They will join several Democratic medical professionals who have been elected since 2018, when a smaller wave of doctors and scientists ran in opposition to President Trump’s first administration.

“You could see a doctors’ caucus here in the Democratic Party,” Dr. Shields said. Just as the candidates were credible on health care to voters, “they’re going to be credible to other senators, or other representatives, once they get into Congress,” he said. He expects that among their top priorities will be making health care through the Affordable Care Act more affordable, perhaps by reinstating the subsidies that expired last year, and streamlining insurance processes to benefit patients.

item.title: Trump Emerges After the Midterms: ‘Did You Guys See the Helipad?’
item.description:
“Now envision chandeliers all over.”

President Trump and his party had just suffered one of the most brutal defeats in modern political history, but when the president emerged before the cameras for the first time, what he wanted to talk to the public about was … home renovation.

“Envision marble floor,” he said. “Oh, it’s going to be beautiful.”

A surreal scene played out on Wednesday as the president led reporters through the White House ballroom to inspect its progress. He pointed out beams, talked about varieties of marble and generally shrugged off what had happened the night before as though it wasn’t the bloodiest political blood bath in this country since 1976 — as though he hadn’t just seen Texas turn blue.

Inside his concrete chrysalis, everything was still beautiful.

“Did you guys see the helipad from up top, how beautiful that is?” he asked.

“The marble is really magnificent marble.”

“It’s a vein that people have been after for 50 years, and the owner of the quarry didn’t want to sell it, but he liked me.”

No malaise. Just marble.

At one point, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum stepped forward and said, “Today, of course, is a day of celebration, and it’s a day of gratitude.”

It was a mirror image of the event that Mr. Burgum and Mr. Trump held the day before the elections, at the foot of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, where Mr. Trump stood inside a plexiglass box and rambled about rusty drainpipes and algae. Many Republicans were frustrated verging on apoplectic that Mr. Trump used his closing message to talk about his pet construction projects. Now the blue crush they feared had come to pass, and Mr. Trump and Mr. Burgum were back at it.

“We’re upgrading trash island,” Mr. Trump informed the press (trash island is what he calls the public golf course on the Potomac River where he dumped rubble from the East Wing).

He was clutching a microphone as he wandered around inside the soaring skeleton of the ballroom. Every so often, the audio feedback from the mike would go haywire, and a cacophonous, screeching sound would go ringing off the massive beams inside the site.

“See the thickness and size of that steel?” he asked as he edged closer to the reporters. He decided to take a few questions.

He didn’t snap at anyone or growl. He didn’t call anybody stupid, fat or ugly. He was placid. He said he wasn’t upset that his vice president was sermonizing on social media about their defeat. He said he didn’t regret going to war with Iran. He said he wouldn’t dump Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. And he defended the speech he gave at the Reflecting Pool on Monday.

“I heard it was a very good speech, got great reviews,” he said. “That was a speech very much like this is today.”

And so it was.

“Watch the beam go up!” Mr. Trump said all of a sudden, cutting off the questions for a time. He ambled toward another corner of the construction site, came to a stop and pointed up to a hole in the ceiling.

The place grew quiet. The reporters stared. A great beam was rising, up through the ballroom, lifted by one of the cranes that has encircled the White House for months. The beam got closer to the hole, but the crane operator couldn’t quite get it out. It was like a game of “Operation,” as the beam kept dinging other pieces of the building’s frame.

Mr. Trump turned and said to no one in particular: “The entire building, every single hole was perfect, which is rare. But we had great people.” The beam made it through the hole. Construction workers clapped.

“Great stuff, right?” the president asked.

He outlined his thinking on the floor plan.

“The kitchen is underneath,” he explained, “because if I put the kitchen on top, and we have large staircases coming from the kitchen, if I put the kitchen on top, you would lose three walls because the kitchen takes about 30 percent of the space.”

Many Republicans inside the Trump administration woke up on Wednesday profoundly depressed, worrying about legal exposure as Democrats contemplate how they will use their new powers on Capitol Hill. Recriminations have already begun. Questions are swirling about who will leave the administration — and what kind of people will be left to take jobs inside going forward.

One close ally of the president working inside the government watched Wednesday’s ballroom tour and concluded that the president was clearly shaken. Another administration official suggested that the president eat a pint of ice cream next time instead of leading a televised tour through a space that for many has become a symbol of why the Grand Old Party went kersplat.

So Republicans looking to the leader of the party on Wednesday to soothe their anxieties might not have been reassured by the ballroom tour. But then, other people’s anxieties might not have been the point.

“It was sort of mentioned a little bit during the campaign: Why does Trump spend time on the White House?” the president said into the microphone, his voice echoing through the construction site. “Well, first of all, it’s very little time. Second of all, I like it. It’s good. For me, it’s relaxing.”

item.title: Susan Collins Finally Falls to an Election Foe: Donald Trump
item.description:
As Susan Collins campaigned in York County, Maine, recently, a woman approached to inform the Republican senator that she had always supported her and “absolutely” loved her. But she wasn’t going to vote for her this time.

“She said it was the only way she could send a message to Trump,” Ms. Collins recounted in an interview on Wednesday, a day after she lost to the Democrat Troy Jackson in her attempt to win a sixth term.

That was the story of the election for Ms. Collins, the chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee and a force in the Senate for three decades.

“I was caught up in the Trump tsunami that swept away many incumbent Republican senators who have served their states well for many years and really care about our country,” she said.

The five-term Republican senator had long seemed invulnerable to the ordinary laws of politics because of her singular political brand as a New England centrist with a gift for constituent service and an ability to steer federal dollars back home. In 2008, she triumphed in Maine while Barack Obama was romping and other Republicans were falling. In 2020, it seemed like her number might be up when polls had her down against a well-funded state lawmaker, but she again won easily.

Democrats saluted ruefully in respect.

But 2026 turned out to be a different case entirely as Ms. Collins was brought down by a combination of factors, most of which were attributable to President Trump and the war with Iran. There were soaring fuel prices in a state reliant on home heating oil. The punishing tariffs the president imposed on neighboring Canada. An immigration crackdown that resulted in a fatal shooting by federal agents in one Maine community. And always the perception that she wasn’t doing enough to stand up to the president, even when she was one of the few Republicans to occasionally break with him.

“Everybody ignores the fact that I voted to convict him in the second impeachment trial,” Ms. Collins said. “What bigger break could there be? It is never enough. I want results and they want angry rhetoric.”

On top of dissatisfaction that she hadn’t distanced herself sufficiently from the president, some voters harbored resentment about her vote in 2018 to confirm Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, given his later role in overturning Roe v. Wade.

The coming result was evident from talking to voters on Tuesday as they exited the central polling place in Bangor — home turf for Ms. Collins. Several of them said they had repeatedly marked their ballots for “our senator,” as her ubiquitous yard signs proclaimed, but they would not do so this time.

“This time,” said Deborah Hanson of Bangor, “I’ve got to try something new. Susan Collins has voted with Trump on so many things.”

“To me, it is a close thing,” said Bob Kelly, another longtime Bangor voter. “But I can’t support anybody that supports Trump.”

In rejecting Ms. Collins, Maine voters gave up a tremendous amount of influence over federal spending by turning out the woman at the helm of the influential committee that controls federal spending. It is unusual but not unheard-of for voters to reject senior leaders.

Voters in Washington State dumped Representative Tom Foley, a Democrat, when he was speaker of the House in 1994. Senator Tom Daschle, the Democratic leader, lost his re-election bid to Senator John Thune, now the majority leader, in South Dakota in 2004.

Ms. Collins leaned heavily on her role in spending as she campaigned around the state, visiting the fire stations, community projects and infrastructure improvements for which she had secured funding, noting that if she were no longer in office, that money might dry up.

“I wanted to make sure people know what their choice was,” she said.

The man who defeated her, Mr. Jackson, will be a junior member of the Senate with little ability to steer to the state anywhere near the kind of financial aid that Ms. Collins had helped win.

“What she has been able to do over the last six years is extraordinary,” said Steve Abbott, her campaign manager and longtime senior aide. “Every town you go to, you see a project that was funded and work that needed to be done. That’s an opportunity that the state has walked away from.”

Up until the end, Ms. Collins and her team had hoped they could pull out a win as they watched from a hotel suite in Bangor. They had been cheered by the “rock star” reception they received around the state, an outpouring they said was better than during some of her winning races in the past.

“We went all over the state and I’ve got to tell you, the crowds were huge, the reception was warm and the response could not have been better,” Ms. Collins said as she addressed and thanked supporters in Bangor before the results were known.

But results from the Democratic stronghold of Portland overwhelmed her.

The race was chaotic, and Ms. Collins and her advisers like to note that they basically had to run against three opponents: Gov. Janet Mills, who initially appeared to be the likely challenger before she dropped out; the oyster farmer Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary but dropped out after sexual abuse allegations; and Mr. Jackson, who had lost the state’s Democratic primary for governor but was then selected to replace Mr. Platner on the ballot.

Democrats have been frustrated for years both by Ms. Collins herself and their inability to defeat her. They poured huge amounts of money into the campaign, trying to highlight her ties to Mr. Trump and her votes for his policies. Ms. Collins pushed back, noting her own differences with the president on the Iran war, tariffs, the immigration crackdown and safety net cuts.

Over the course of her career, Ms. Collins was at the center of many major legislative negotiations on such tough issues as gun safety, health care and, following the Jan. 6, 2021, assault at the Capitol, a bill overhauling how electoral votes were counted. Her absence in the Senate will be felt on big legislative fights. She has not missed a vote in her Senate tenure.

Her political career was inspired in part by Margaret Chase Smith, the Maine Republican who served in the Senate from 1949 to 1972. Ms. Collins once met Ms. Smith, who had delivered a famous denunciation of Joseph McCarthy, and noted that some constituents encouraged her to have a Smith-like moment of conscience when it came to Mr. Trump.

“I would argue that I have, like Margaret Chase Smith, taken a lot of tough votes and stood up for what I believe in,” she said. “But I think the best comparison is we each lost our last race for the Senate.

“I have now had my Margaret Chase Smith moment.”
