item.title: His Senate Win Is Big to Muslim Americans, but Not Because of Faith
item.description:
When Karrar Al-Sadkhan, 18, cast his first-ever ballot on Tuesday at a middle school in Dearborn, Mich., he chose a fellow Muslim to be his state’s next senator.

But while his pick, Abdul El-Sayed, defied a crush of anti-Muslim attacks and was elected as America’s first Muslim senator, for Mr. Al-Sadkhan, religion had little to do with it.

“The Democratic side was more focused on gas and health care and grocery prices, so that motivated me,” he said. “The Constitution gives us the freedom to worship how we want, but we still have allegiance to the Constitution.”

Mr. El-Sayed’s victory is a watershed moment for American Muslims, and a complicated one. It solidifies the community’s rising influence in national American politics even as Islamophobia is also surging in some quarters, backlash to which most likely contributed to his success.

Yet in interviews, Muslim voters from Illinois to Michigan to Washington, D.C., said they did not see his win as significant because he shares their faith. Instead, many see Mr. El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, not primarily as a religious touchstone, but as part of a progressive Democratic coalition taking root across the country, one that prioritizes things like affordability, universal health care and ending U.S. funding for Israel.

“Our country isn’t an Islamic-based nation,” said Mohamad Saab, 23, a college student who also voted for Mr. El-Sayed in Dearborn. “It’s a secular nation, and we want it to be that way.”

On the campaign trail, Mr. El-Sayed sought to challenge notions of what modern religious extremism looks like in America, noting that conservative Christian lawmakers have made explicit efforts to dismantle the separation of church and state.

At a town hall two weeks ago, a young man confronted Mr. El-Sayed, asking him to disavow the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist political group, which he did. Mr. El-Sayed then asked the man, who described himself as a Christian, if he, too, would disavow “any attempt to read any religious doctrine into the laws of our country.”

The man, who formerly worked for Senator Josh Hawley, a conservative Republican, said he would not.

Mr. El-Sayed replied, “I think it’s you who needs to understand the Constitution, not me.” The hall erupted in cheers.

In Washington on Tuesday, Nesrin Abaza, 65, offered free coffee to anyone who displayed an “I Voted” sticker at her Palestinian restaurant. Any focus on Mr. El-Sayed’s religion is “ridiculous,” she said. Instead, she sees him as part of an ascendant group of young Democrats, including Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and James Talarico, who won the Texas Senate race on Tuesday.

“I support a new democratic movement,” Ms. Abaza said. “We are tired of people not listening to us.”

In Skokie, Ill., Bushra Amiwala, 28, said she did not think about the fact that Mr. El-Sayed is Muslim like she is, or about his criticism of Israel. Instead, Ms. Amiwala, an elected member of her city’s school board, hopes he will continue to advocate values she shares, like protecting women’s reproductive rights and investing in local schools.

“Money out of politics, money in your pockets and Medicare for all,” she said. “That’s all I hear Abdul say, to be honest.”

Momentum for Mr. El-Sayed has been building since New Yorkers last year elected Zohran Mamdani as the city’s first Muslim mayor and the country’s highest-level Muslim executive.

Muslim supporters were part of the Democratic coalition that helped lift both Mr. El-Sayed and Mr. Mamdani to victory. But overall, the Democratic Party has become more religiously unaffiliated as it also becomes less Christian.

Mr. El-Sayed worked to appeal across those changing demographics.

Late in the campaign, he released an ad highlighting himself not as a Muslim but as a “man of faith,” noting that his name means “servant” and that he prays every day. .

Republicans pummeled Mr. El-Sayed with racist and anti-Muslim attacks throughout his campaign. His Republican opponent, former Representative Mike Rogers, tried to connect his mother to Al Qaeda. President Trump called him a “vicious, violent jihadist,” claimed his victory would bring a wave of jihadists to America and described him as an enemy of Christians who would end Christmas.

Those attacks most likely contributed to Mr. El-Sayed’s success with Muslim voters.

“They helped us mobilize the community like never before,” said Basim Elkarra, senior adviser to the Unity and Justice Fund, a group that knocked on 135,000 doors for Mr. El-Sayed in Detroit neighborhoods with large Muslim and Middle Eastern populations.

As he canvassed voters, Mr. Elkarra often told them about recent cases in which a Muslim candidate lost by narrow margins — including, in one local Illinois election last year, by a single vote.

“The issue of Gaza is important to so many community members,” he said, noting an issue that resonated with many Democrats even as it alienated many Jewish voters.

Mr. El-Sayed has suggested Israel does not have the right to exist as a Jewish state, though he softened that position near the end of his campaign. Michigan’s other senator, the Democrat Elissa Slotkin, is Jewish.

Despite Mr. El-Sayed’s success, American views on Islam are more negative and partisan now than they were after Sept. 11. Seventy-six percent of Republicans believe that Islam is more likely than other religions to encourage violence, up from 32 percent in early 2002, according to the Pew Research Center. For Democrats, the share rose to 29 percent from 23.

In Texas, Republican lawmakers — including Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton, who both lost their races on Tuesday — have investigated Muslim institutions and restricted the public practice of Islam, even as their state mandated Bible readings in public schools.

Andy Nguyen, 40, who voted for Mr. Talarico at a large mosque in Sugar Land, Texas, said he believed that Mr. El-Sayed and Mr. Mamdani want to work to benefit all citizens, expressing hope that their actions will help dispel anti-Muslim sentiment.

“Maybe with these two gentlemen, people will begin to open their eyes and feel differently,” said Mr. Nguyen, a dentist who converted to Islam in 2023.

Azar Mohammed, 53, became a U.S. citizen in 2023 and voted for the first time this year, for a straight Democratic ticket and for pragmatic reasons.

A contractor in Richardson, Texas, who employs a largely Latino work force, Mr. Mohammed said he was dismayed by the impact of President Trump’s immigration crackdown on his employees.

“We came here to work. We contribute to this country with our taxes. We work hard,” said Mr. Mohammed, who emigrated from India 33 years ago.

Muslims make up about 1 percent of the U.S. population, according to Pew. They historically align more with the Democratic Party but have recently become a more fluid cohort, including in Michigan in 2024, when Arab American voters expressed frustration over the Biden administration’s support for Israel and helped deliver the state for Mr. Trump.

In Clarkston, Ga., a suburb of Atlanta known as a haven for refugees, Khushal Gurbaz, 41, a limo driver, voted for Jon Ossoff because he wanted an end to the war with Iran.

Yet he also voted for Rick Jackson, his state’s Republican candidate for governor, thinking he would combat crime more adeptly than the Democrat, Keisha Lance Bottoms, who ultimately won.

Mr. El-Sayed was not the only Muslim candidate who won on Tuesday; Adam Hamawy, a New Jersey Democrat, was elected to the U.S. House, as was Darializa Avila Chevalier, a recent convert and democratic socialist, from New York.

Noting that many Americans still have a level of discomfort with Islam, Zeenat Rahman, executive director of the Institute of Politics at the University of Chicago, said Mr. El-Sayed and other newly elected Muslims would be closely scrutinized.

“How he governs will matter,” she said. “Our politicians who are Muslim American have a really big responsibility.”

For now, Wafic Faour, 66, a Palestinian American Muslim in Vermont, felt a sense of hope and pride when he took in the results.

It was proof that voters believe Muslims constructively add to the American project, he said.

“Islam tells you to look at your neighbor the same way you look at yourself, to help other people,” he said.

Reporting was contributed by Ken Fountain from Missouri City, Texas, Ryan Hooper from Dearborn, Mich., Johnny Kauffman from Clarkston, Ga., Carolyn Shapiro from Burlington, Vt., and Sasha von Oldershausen from Richardson, Texas.

item.title: G.O.P. Group Says Party Faces a ‘Crisis-Level’ Loss of Elected Women
item.description:
A group that champions electing conservative women to public office issued a blunt warning to Republicans on Wednesday after the Democratic sweep of Congress, calling the defeats of a large number of G.O.P. women an emergency that must be addressed.

“We are once again facing a crisis-level decline in Republican women in Congress,” Danielle Barrow, the president of Winning For Women Action Fund, an outside group dedicated to electing Republican women, said in a statement.

Ms. Barrow sounded the alarm as Democrats were celebrating their own milestone of electing more than 100 women to the House for the first time in history.

Republicans already have far less gender diversity in their ranks in the House, where there are currently 32 G.O.P. women (including two nonvoting delegates) — around 15 percent of their members.

With the landslide Democratic victories that are projected to win them the largest House majority in decades, that number could potentially dip to below 20 next year, after all races are called.

In 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected just one new G.O.P. woman to Congress, the party made a commitment to recruit and invest in female candidates, Ms. Barrow said. It worked: Two years later, 11 of the 15 seats Republicans flipped were by women.

“But that commitment to recruiting women faded when the urgency did,” she said. “Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve. It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

item.title: Trump Wrestles With New Reality: A Lame Duck With Two Years Left to Fight
item.description:
Over the course of his life, Donald J. Trump has readily embraced many identities: A hotel developer. A reality television star. A president. A firebrand.

Now, at 80 years old, he is confronting one he would rather not: a lame duck.

In the hours after voters put a check on the expansive power he has flexed in his second term, giving Democrats control of both the House and the Senate, Mr. Trump seemed to be cycling through the stages of grief. He denied that a blue wave across the country had been his fault, or a direct result of his decision to go to war with Iran. (The vice president explicitly said otherwise.) He accepted the election results. And, as he absorbed the waning power he will have in his final two years in office, he bargained, saying he’d work with Democrats while clinging to his veto Sharpie.

“I’ll get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive,” Mr. Trump told reporters on Wednesday, standing in front of a steel beam that was being put into place as part of his cherished White House ballroom project.

He noted that he had “the power to veto,” before turning to a topic he seemed much more eager to discuss: his renovation projects.

Whether Mr. Trump adopts a pragmatic deal-making posture remains to be seen — one ally described the president as “dazed” after the rout on Tuesday.

After his loss in the 2020 presidential race, the last major political setback Mr. Trump confronted, he retreated to Mar-a-Lago, where he nursed his anger and then planned a defiant return. Once back in the White House, Mr. Trump had no use for compromise.

After a period spent as a political pariah and criminal defendant, Mr. Trump liked to say that he had gone from hunted to hunter. In his second term, his administration has tracked down his political enemies, unleashed a violent immigration crackdown and started a war that has made life more expensive for Americans. He didn’t need Congress to do any of it.

But on Tuesday, that dynamic flipped again. Democrats are vowing to investigate government abuses, alleged corruption by the president’s associates and the heavy-handed tactics of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. House lawmakers plan to scrutinize top officials involved in the administration’s immigration agenda, including the White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller; Tom Homan, Mr. Trump’s border czar; and the homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, according to a person with knowledge of the discussions.

“LAWYER UP,” Representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat poised to lead the House Oversight Committee, wrote on social media.

The political pressure could make for an unpredictable two years for both Mr. Trump and the country, according to people who have observed firsthand his volatile personality and his refusal to acknowledge mistakes.

“When you look at things like his ability to do executive orders and grant pardons and all of these things, he’s going to still be doing enormous damage,” said Sarah Matthews, a former White House deputy press secretary who resigned after the attack on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. “And it’s just going to get even more chaotic and dangerous in these next two years.”

Political rivals believe that Mr. Trump, who has asserted his dominance over the Republican Party for the better part of the last decade, will also do everything to maintain his grip on a party that he effectively reshaped in his image.

“Donald Trump needs attention like most people need oxygen,” said former Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey, a Republican who is considering another presidential run in 2028. “He can’t do without it, and he’s now going to experience for the first time in his political career being a lame duck. So what he’ll need to do is to act out even more than he normally does in order to divert you from the 2028 race.”

Mr. Trump has so far been vague about how he wants to spend the next two years, telling the podcaster and former top F.B.I. official Dan Bongino in an interview on Tuesday that he has “many, many things in the hopper.”

He did not elaborate and instead pivoted into a standard part of his stump speech: “You know, right now we have more factories and plants being built in the United States than at any time ever before, and that means the Roaring Twenties, that means every — there’s never been anything like it.” (Manufacturing has actually slowed since 2024, according to the National Association of Manufacturers.)

He suggested in interviews that he might seek to join forces with his political opponents on the debt ceiling and immigration enforcement — two thorny policy issues that have bedeviled past administrations.

And he repeatedly invoked his ability to veto legislation, implicitly underscoring how much he will be on defense in his last two years in office.

In his first public appearance after Election Day, Mr. Trump stood before reporters at the White House on Wednesday and talked not about any lessons learned, or the path forward for the Republican Party. Instead, he mused about his ballroom project and his own future, particularly the subject of impeachment.

“I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that — impeachment for no reason,” Mr. Trump said. “What, for having a successful country? Our country is more successful now than at any time in history.”

He paused, turning his focus back on the ballroom construction.

“Watch the beam go up,” he said. “Now envision chandeliers all over.”

Several top aides had already been planning for what Mr. Trump could accomplish through executive power alone if Republicans lost one or both chambers of Congress. Those involved include Mr. Miller; Russell T. Vought, the White House budget director; and members of the White House legislative affairs staff, according to a White House official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal discussions. The president would receive a “menu of options” soon, the person said.

A hushed conversation of what comes next for Mr. Trump’s presidency and those around him played out on Tuesday night inside the White House, where Mr. Trump gathered aides and cabinet members in the East Room for what turned into a morose watch party. As the president watched the returns and fielded phone calls, some of the people around him quietly discussed whether Mr. Trump would keep in place members of his cabinet or his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, according to two people who attended.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Administration officials and Mr. Trump’s allies said the president and his staff were girding themselves for both congressional investigations and high turnover for the remainder of his time in office.

Some expressed anxiety that there had been little guidance for staff about what to do if they got pulled into investigations, other than a briefing earlier this year advising them generally how to respond to congressional oversight.

As the political conversation turns to the next cycle, Mr. Trump indicated that he was not ready to name a political heir or back a candidate to succeed him in 2028. Asked by Martha MacCallum of Fox News late Tuesday evening whether he wanted a Republican primary to determine the 2028 presidential nominee, the president said, “I think it’s going to end up being somewhat of that.”

By Wednesday morning, Vice President JD Vance had posted a lengthy message on social media placing blame for Republican losses on the decision to go to war with Iran, an apparent effort to separate himself from Mr. Trump.

Several people close to the president say they believe that he is unlikely to endorse Mr. Vance — or anyone else — anytime soon. Mr. Trump is an entertainer above all, they say, and he will want to stay in the spotlight.

Zolan Kanno-Youngs contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: What We Know (and Don’t Know) in the Alaska and Mississippi Senate Vote Counts
item.description:
Control of the U.S. Senate has already been determined, with 33 of the 35 contests being called within hours of polls closing. In Alaska and Mississippi, however, no race calls have been made for the Senate and it could be quite some time until either contest is decided, even as some additional vote totals trickle out in the coming days.

In both cases, the Democratic nominee is clinging to a slim lead, but the reasons for the lack of a call are far different.

Alaska’s Senate race could take days or weeks to be called. Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, had a lead of fewer than 1,000 votes as of Wednesday afternoon, but nearly a quarter of the expected votes remain uncounted.

The bulk of the remaining vote is in the form of mail-in ballots. Some were cast close to Election Day, while others were postmarked by Election Day and will be received in the days after. A smaller chunk of early in-person ballots are also outstanding.

The deadline to tabulate all ballots, including provisional ballots, is Nov. 18. That is also the date that ranked-choice tabulation will begin, should neither Ms. Peltola nor Senator Daniel S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, cross the 50 percent threshold needed to win the election in the first round.

While the late mail vote typically leans toward Democrats, multiple factors could undercut Ms. Peltola’s possible advantage, including how many ballots will be received and how many are from voters who did not rank additional candidates beyond their first choice. There is also the potentially confounding presence of the other two candidates on the ballot, Gerald L. Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

A New York Times analysis of the available ranked-choice data pulled from each voter’s ballot shows that more than a third of voters who ranked Mr. Heikes or Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. as their first choice did not rank another candidate. That means these ballots would not count toward either Ms. Peltola or Senator Sullivan in subsequent rounds of the ranked-choice tabulation.

As of Wednesday evening, Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee in Mississippi, had a lead of roughly 1,000 votes over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent. Because the margin is so tight, The Associated Press may not be able to make a race call until the state certifies a winner.

Mississippi is somewhat of an outlier in that it does not have a mechanism for automatic recounts, and has no method for a candidate to contest the election, so a court order would be required to initiate a recount.

Nearly all of the votes have been counted in the race, but a smattering of provisional ballots — which are ballots given to those with questions about their eligibility to vote — are still waiting to be counted, as are some late-arriving mail ballots. According to Mississippi's secretary of state, there are approximately 3,600 outstanding mail ballots that could arrive in time to be counted.

Mississippi’s Supreme Court ruled in June that the state must accept mail-in ballots that arrive by the Tuesday after Election Day — this year, Nov. 10. And provisional ballots in the state must be tallied by that day as well. For a provisional ballot to be accepted, the voter is required to provide proper identification to elections officials, obtain a state voter ID card, or submit a religious exemption.

Some counties in the state have said they hope to begin releasing some results of provisional ballots on Wednesday. It is currently unknown how many ballots remain uncounted statewide. Adding a layer of complexity, ballot processing and counting, which includes ruling on provisional ballots, is conducted by each county’s five-person elections commission rather than a single elections official.

In 2024, the state had just under 15,000 provisional ballots, of which 70 percent were accepted. In 2022, the state had about 5,700 provisional ballots, of which 75 percent were accepted.

Evan Peng contributed reporting.

item.title: Justice Alito Will Not Retire Immediately, Despite Election Outcome
item.description:
Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. has told people close to him that he does not intend to retire immediately from the Supreme Court, despite Democrats’ commanding win in Senate contests on Tuesday, which means Republicans will hold the chamber for only a short time longer.

As a result, Republicans may have missed the window for President Trump to name a fourth or even a fifth justice to the Supreme Court in the final two years of his presidency.

Justice Alito shared his plans with friends after the election results were clear this week, according to two people close to the justice who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

As recently as last month, Justice Alito, a forceful conservative and reliable vote in favor of Mr. Trump’s policies, had rejected the idea that he would step down if Democrats took control of the Senate.

“I intend to stick around through this term,” he told Bloomberg News, in an interview published in early October.

But the state of the electoral map after Tuesday’s election generated speculation that he or Justice Clarence Thomas — the court’s two oldest justices — could quickly announce their retirements and give the president a brief window to push through a successor during the Senate’s lame-duck session.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Over the years, Justice Thomas has ruled out retiring, suggesting he would serve for decades more. With 35 years on the bench, if Justice Thomas were to stay through May 2028, he would set the record as the longest-serving justice in Supreme Court history.

Justice Thomas, who is 78, and Justice Alito, who is 76, did not respond to requests for comment about their plans.

Despite the public conversation, legal experts were largely agreed on Wednesday that a speedy retirement would be a potentially dicey and problematic proposition that was not guaranteed to secure a seat.

A nominee would have faced the newfound independence of departing Republican senators such as John Cornyn of Texas and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who were defeated in primaries by Trump-backed challengers, in addition to Susan Collins of Maine, a moderate who lost on Tuesday. The group may have had little appetite to help Mr. Trump ram through a nominee of his choice.

After Mr. Trump won re-election in 2024, the conservative legal analyst Ed Whelan said that he expected Justice Alito to announce his retirement the next spring and predicted that Justice Thomas would step down in 2026. The moves, he had believed, would allow Mr. Trump to replace the justices with younger jurists who might secure the court’s conservative supermajority for a generation.

Of course, an unexpected vacancy due to health concerns, for instance, could arise at any time during the remainder of Mr. Trump’s tenure. But after Tuesday’s election, in which the scale of the Democrats’ win in Congress was larger than expected, Mr. Whelan said the two conservative justices now may not be able to retire before 2033 if they want to be succeeded by a nominee with a similar judicial philosophy.

“No justice is going to announce in the next few days that he will be stepping down,” Mr. Whelan wrote, adding, “Justices don’t make snap decisions about retiring.”

Robert Luther III, a professor at Antonin Scalia Law School who helped choose Mr. Trump’s judicial nominees during his first term, agreed.

“I don’t anticipate any retirements before January, and frankly, I wouldn’t advise it,” he said.

Both justices were on the bench when Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg decided not to retire before the 2016 election, a decision many court observers consider a cautionary tale. Instead of allowing President Barack Obama to pick her successor, Justice Ginsburg died while in office in 2020, creating an opening for Mr. Trump to replace the liberal icon with a conservative, Justice Amy Coney Barrett.

But now, conservatives fret that both men may be in danger of following Justice Ginsburg’s example. If a Democrat were elected to succeed Mr. Trump as president in 2028, both Justices Alito and Thomas would be in their 80s before a Republican could regain the White House and be in position to nominate a successor. Forecasts for when the G.O.P. might regain control of the Senate are even cloudier.

At the end of the Supreme Court’s last term in June, speculation had intensified about Justice Alito’s future and whether Mr. Trump would have an opening to continue to remake a Supreme Court that already includes three of his first-term nominees.

Because of Justice Thomas’s previous statements, attention centered on Justice Alito. It reached a fever pitch on the last day of the term when NPR erroneously reported, and then retracted, his retirement.

In a series of interviews published in October, Justice Alito acknowledged that he had “thought about” retiring at the end of the term, but said he had ruled it out, thinking he could still make a “valuable contribution,” as he told CBS News.

Meanwhile, a newly empowered Democratic Congress will have other implications for the Supreme Court beyond vacancies and nominations. Democrats unhappy with rulings from the conservative bench have repeatedly called for changing the structure of the court. Recent polls show bipartisan support for enacting an enforcement mechanism for the ethics code the justices adopted in 2023, and for eliminating life tenure for justices.

Gabe Roth of Fix the Court, which advocates judicial accountability, predicted on Wednesday that House and Senate committees overseeing the courts would also revive judicial ethics investigations that were largely paused two years ago.

Justice Thomas, for one, could face renewed questions surrounding gifts he accepted, but initially did not report, from his friend Harlan Crow, a Texas billionaire and Republican donor. The justice has said he was not required to report such gifts at the time.

Abbie VanSickle and Michael Gold contributed reporting.

item.title: How Kansas Democrats Laid the Groundwork for a Historic Senate Upset
item.description:
On an Election Day with historic Democratic victories across several conservative states, one of the most momentous happened in Kansas, where Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate election in nearly a century.

But Kansas Democrats have been slowly rising from political oblivion for years, laying the groundwork for Tuesday, when a strong candidate, a beatable incumbent and an auspicious national environment converged.

Despite its ruby-red reputation, cemented in the 2004 book “What’s the Matter With Kansas?”, the state has a two-term Democratic governor, a Democratic congresswoman and an electorate that backed abortion rights in a statewide vote. In addition to Mr. Hamilton’s victory, Democrats held narrow leads on Wednesday in elections for governor and attorney general in races that have not been called.

“This wasn’t an overnight success or an overnight accident,” said Representative Sharice Davids, a Democrat who flipped a congressional seat in Kansas in 2018 and who won re-election on Tuesday by more than 20 percentage points. “This was the culmination of literally almost a full decade of us working hard.”

Entering this year, Kansas was at the center of the Senate map only in the geographic sense. Few expected Senator Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent, to lose his seat.

But Mr. Hamilton, a moderate Democrat, changed the political landscape when he entered the race. He had strong name recognition in the Kansas City suburbs, where the United Methodist congregation that he started has grown into a megachurch. And he proved to be a skilled messenger and fund-raiser on the campaign trail.

Mr. Marshall, a doctor and first-term senator who aligned himself closely with President Trump, was the ideal opponent. He faced scrutiny for his frequent trips to Florida. And he struggled to respond to criticism after The New York Times reported that, as a doctor, he often sued his patients over medical debts, leading to dozens of them being arrested.

“You’re not always going to have the perfect environment, the perfect candidate, a weak opponent — all of the things align for you,” said Ashley All, a longtime Democratic strategist in Kansas. “But if you do the work and you prepare, and you invest in building those relationships with different voters and building back trust, then you have a chance.”

Kansas Republicans were still assessing their losses on Wednesday.

In addition to statewide races still in play, Democrats flipped several seats in the Kansas House of Representatives. Some heavily Hispanic counties with large meatpacking plants accounted for the largest shifts away from Republicans after a recent immigration enforcement campaign in those areas alarmed even some of the president’s usual allies.

But many of the same economic themes that resounded across the country, as Democrats won races in several bright-red states, were also driving the conversation in Kansas.

“National issues played a bigger part in Kansas politics in the outcome than ever before,” said Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat barred by term limits from running again.

State Senator Mike Thompson, a Republican from the Kansas City suburbs, said voters were “sending messages to us that we want this economy straightened up, and I think that’s lesson learned.” High diesel prices and tariffs were areas of voter concern, he said.

State Representative Pat Proctor, a Republican, said that he thought “Kansas just got caught in the national winds.”

He said the effort “to turn out very, very angry and disgruntled Democrats and left-leaning independents was just so overwhelming that it shifted the entire electorate.”

Not all was lost for Republicans. Mr. Proctor, his party’s nominee for secretary of state, was leading in a narrow race on Wednesday. Republicans will also retain a supermajority in the Kansas Senate, where most seats were not up for election.

Still, Kansas Republicans are not used to losing in such spectacular fashion.

No Democratic presidential candidate has carried the state since Lyndon B. Johnson in the 1960s. And while past U.S. Senate races — including in 2014 and 2020 — had generated hopes of breaking Republicans’ 94-year winning streak in that chamber, liberals ended up disappointed.

The seeds of Tuesday’s results were planted in Kansas in 2018, during the first Trump midterm, when Ms. Kelly flipped the governorship and Ms. Davids flipped her House seat. Both candidates benefited from stronger-than-usual performances in Johnson County, just outside Kansas City, a former Republican stronghold that has since become the engine of Democrats’ statewide relevance.

Mr. Hamilton and State Senator Cindy Holscher, the Democratic nominee for governor, are both from Johnson County, the state’s most populous county, and both were leading there by more than 20 percentage points.

“We have built an infrastructure in Johnson County,” said State Representative Mari-Lynn Poskin, a Democrat who flipped a legislative seat in the county in 2020 and described years of work to staff a party office, fill precinct-level roles and step up door-knocking efforts. It was not that many years ago, she and the governor said, that there was not even a permanent Democratic Party office there.

Ms. Kelly, who expressed confidence that the close races for governor and attorney general would ultimately be called for Democrats, said she was “on cloud nine” on Wednesday. She said having Mr. Hamilton in Washington will give Kansans a senator who will “stand for them and their real values.”

Like other Democratic officials, she expressed hope that Tuesday was not a fleeting high-water mark for her party, but rather a sign of a durable political shift — a counterpoint to anyone who had written her state off as permanently Republican.

“You know the book, ‘What’s the Matter With Kansas?’” Governor Kelly said on Wednesday. “We rewrote it.”

item.title: These Republicans Bet Big on Trump. It Didn’t Pay Off.
item.description:
President Trump used to gloat about his near-perfect endorsement record, reveling in the control he exerted over the Republican nomination process during this year’s primary season. Voters overwhelmingly rewarded the candidates he backed and punished those who displeased him, muscling numerous less loyal candidates out of contention.

“If you pushed back” on Mr. Trump, said Justin Evans, a Republican strategist in South Carolina, “you’d get your head chopped off.”

Mr. Trump has little to brag about this week. Senate candidates he had helped elevate, including Darline Graham in South Carolina, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and Ken Paxton in Texas, lost by margins previously unimagined by even the most optimistic Democrats. Those high-profile defeats contributed to what Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida, a one-time Trump rival for the presidential nomination, called as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans” as the country has seen in a century.

“The people who did the best last night were the people who distanced themselves from the president,” Mr. Evans said, calling the results “a universal repudiation of the bullying that’s been taking place during this primary” by Mr. Trump.

Here’s a look at what happened to some of the candidates who tied their fortunes most closely to Mr. Trump.

After Senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican, died in July, Mr. Trump threw his weight behind Mr. Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, in a snap primary election. While many Republican insiders objected, primary voters listened, narrowly nominating Ms. Graham over Representative Ralph Norman, despite her self-described lack of experience or policy expertise.

On Tuesday, the wider South Carolina electorate rejected Ms. Graham, choosing to send a Democrat to Washington for the first time in nearly 30 years.

“It wasn’t that voters rebuked Trump,” Mr. Evans said, noting that the Republican nominee for governor had earned at least 90,000 more votes than Ms. Graham. “It was that the entire Washington machine pushed this woman on South Carolina, and South Carolina resoundingly pushed back.”

Senate Republicans begged Mr. Trump to endorse Senator John Cornyn over Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, in the state’s Republican Senate primary. Many argued that Mr. Paxton’s scandal-ridden past would make it significantly more difficult, and more costly, to win in a general election. They also said a contentious intraparty battle would waste resources needed in more competitive states. Mr. Trump ignored them, waiting until days before a May primary runoff to back Mr. Paxton.

On Tuesday, despite dramatically outspending Democrats, Republicans lost the Senate seat, the governor’s mansion, and every other statewide race in Texas, breaking a more than three-decade-long streak of G.O.P. dominance.

Some Texas Republicans speculated that Mr. Paxton would have won the primary regardless of Mr. Trump’s choice. It is also not clear that Mr. Cornyn could have defied the tsunami of voter anger that propelled Democrats to victory up and down the ballot. But some blamed Mr. Paxton, and Mr. Trump, for the extent of the losses.

“You stand by Trump at your own peril at this point,” said Dade Phelan, the former Republican speaker of the State House. He recalled how Mr. Trump asked voters in Texas and elsewhere to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

“Well, voters imagined he was on the ballot,” Mr. Phelan said. “And it was an absolute apocalypse for Republicans.”

Mr. Trump’s fingerprints were all over North Carolina’s Senate race. First, Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who has served in North Carolina for more than a decade, announced he would retire rather than run for re-election after the president threatened to back a primary opponent against him.

Then, Mr. Trump handpicked Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chairman, and Mr. Whatley spent millions touting Mr. Trump’s endorsement ahead of his victory in the Republican Senate primary. On Tuesday night, Mr. Whatley fell to former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, by around 20 points, a stunning leftward shift for a state that Mr. Trump won in 2024.

Meghan McMichael, 33, a voter in Canton, N.C., said on Tuesday that she had voted for Mr. Cooper and other Democrats in order to hold the Trump administration accountable for its treatment of immigrants, and the state of the economy.

“I’m just hopeful that certain people will be held accountable for things that have happened over the last two years,” she said.

Senator Jon Husted, Ohio’s Republican Senate nominee and a former professional football player, was little known nationally until President Trump started talking about his rear end while on the campaign trail. Mr. Husted also joined Mr. Trump at several Ohio rallies in the final weeks of the campaign, tying himself to the president.

Mr. Husted lost to former Senator Sherrod Brown on Tuesday, making Ohio one of seven states that Democrats had flipped as of Wednesday evening.

The president’s comments about Mr. Husted’s backside may also have backfired, with voters across the country telling The New York Times they had disapproved of his remarks that Mr. Husted had a “great ass” and a “pile of muscle.”

In Lincoln, Neb., on Tuesday, Deondre Webster, 36, said he didn’t believe Mr. Trump is a good role model for his three daughters.

“We don’t want to see the leader of the country talking about male behinds or stuff like that onstage,” he said. “When he’s supposed to be the leader, and that’s not what we’re teaching our kids.”

Mark Barrett in North Carolina and Justin Diep in Nebraska contributed reporting.

item.title: San Francisco’s Favorite Start-Up, the Valkyries, Is All Human, No A.I.
item.description:
The motorcycle club Dykes on Bikes revved their engines. Low riders bobbed in celebration. Nancy Pelosi, in a violet suit to match her violet stilettos, waved a rally towel from a motorized cable car.

In boom-time San Francisco, there are many unicorns, the name for privately owned start-ups worth at least $1 billion. But only one got a victory parade on Wednesday — and a quintessentially Bay Area one at that.

The guests of honor were not tech bros unleashing artificial intelligence agents. They were the Golden State Valkyries, the new champions of the Women’s National Basketball Association, who played their first game just 18 months ago.

Already, the billionaire venture capitalist Joe Lacob’s investment of $50 million to buy the rights to a Bay Area expansion team has ballooned to a $1 billion valuation, a record for a women’s sports team. After the championship, Mr. Lacob said, “A V.C. friend has told me this is the best start-up he’s ever seen.”

The Valkyries have sold out every game they have played at Chase Center, the waterfront arena that also hosts the Golden State Warriors. Their nail-biting Game 7 win over the Atlanta Dream to take the trophy on Saturday night drew 3.3 million viewers, the most of any W.N.B.A. playoff game ever.

But the numbers do not tell the full picture. Love stories, after all, do not revolve around data — and San Francisco and the wider Bay Area have fallen hard for the Valkyries.

On Wednesday, hundreds of thousands of fans lined the Embarcadero, the waterfront boulevard studded with palm trees. They filled the wide sidewalks from the Ferry Building and southward for blocks. They screamed with glee as the team, most of them women of color and several of them queer, began rolling past on double-decker, open-air tourist buses painted violet.

Stacey Camillo, 62, dressed as an actual Valkyrie, a woman warrior from Norse mythology, carrying a sword and wearing a gold headpiece. She said she ran track in college, but there was no hope back then of young women becoming professional athletes. She said she had been waiting decades for a moment like this one.

Ms. Camillo, who is lesbian, said the fact that the team’s players and coach had spoken out in support of gay and transgender people throughout the season made their win even more special.

“The team embodies the best of the Bay Area in terms of support and community and social justice,” she said.

The coincidental timing of the parade — hours after Democrats routed Republicans and elected numerous women, people of color and transgender candidates to office — seemed to infuse the deep-blue city with even more joy. One fan carried a sign reading, “No Kings! Only Valkyries.”

As he kicked off the parade, Mayor Daniel Lurie said, “The sun is shining down on our city, and yes, our country!”

The crowd cheered even louder.

It was one more big win for a city that had been counted out just five years ago after the pandemic hollowed out its downtown, the fentanyl epidemic killed thousands and property crime surged. Those challenges have eased, and San Francisco’s biggest problem now is that so many people, particularly those working in A.I., want to live in the city, driving housing prices way up.

“It’s a championship that reflects San Francisco’s comeback and reflects the Bay Area’s rise,” Mr. Lurie said. He said its importance to the city recalled the January 1982 Super Bowl win by the San Francisco 49ers, which came as the AIDS epidemic was beginning and soon after the assassinations of Supervisor Harvey Milk and Mayor George Moscone.

San Francisco is now bathed in violet, the team’s color, from lights atop the City Hall dome and the Transamerica Pyramid to the gear sported by legions of fans.

The Muni buses’ destination signs read “Go Valkyries!” The airport had big violet displays featuring basketballs in its terminals. The libraries are issuing special Valkyries library cards.

There is a waiting list for season tickets for next year at Chase Center, which is called Ballhalla when the Valkyries play, a twist on Valhalla, the hall of the slain in Norse mythology.

On a BART train to the parade, Fatima Ramirez, 36, said she told the teacher of her 8-year-old son, Victor, that he would miss school because of a stuffy nose, but she was actually taking him to the parade.

“You have to go to a parade if there’s a parade,” Victor, a third grader in a Valkyries cap, explained.

Ms. Ramirez attended the 2012 victory parade for the San Francisco Giants, but said she was more excited about this one.

“In a space with so many women, it just hits different,” she said. “It’s a big testament to what happens when you support women in sports.”

She rested her hand on her pregnant belly, and said her baby girl, whom she has already named Elsie, is due in a few weeks. She said someday she will show the parade photos to Elsie and tell her how important it was that she was there.

item.title: Immigration Tactics Motivated Voters, Near and Far From Southern Border
item.description:
Alongside the flowers, placards and other mementos placed at memorial sites honoring people killed by federal immigration agents in Houston, Minneapolis, and Biddeford, Maine, a new tribute appeared this week: “I Voted” stickers.

Immigration and the Trump administration’s confrontational enforcement campaign emerged as one of the most divisive and emotionally charged issues driving voters to the polls, according to interviews with dozens of voters before and after Election Day.

Yet unlike in the election cycles since President Trump’s campaign in 2016, the conversation was no longer an abstract debate about chaos at the southern border.

Aggressive federal operations in cities, suburban neighborhoods and rural job sites across America disrupted morning commutes, grocery runs and daily routines, turning workplaces, residential streets and civic buildings into sites of volatile encounters.

“Saying he was going to secure the border is one of the reasons Trump got elected,” said Peter Polos, 73, a physician from Basking Ridge, N.J., who cast his ballot for the Democrat in a battleground House race in his home state. “But he didn’t say he was going to secure the border by knocking people down in the street, throwing them in a car, and taking them away.”

Democrats counted the Trump administration’s approach to immigration among the top issues that fueled their seismic victories across the country. Beneath those electoral gains, political strategists and pollsters from both parties suggested the shift had less to do with the Democrats’ vision for immigration policy and instead was a referendum on the administration’s aggressive enforcement tactics.

“It was a clear rebuke of Republican immigration politics, of the cruelty, of the disdain for brown skin,” said Julián Castro, a former Obama official and former mayor of San Antonio.

High-profile and sometimes deadly incidents brought the administration’s enforcement methods into sharp focus.

In Minnesota, where the Trump administration carried out Operation Metro Surge in January, federal agents clashed with bystanders near schools, detained residents with lawful status, and shot and killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti, two U.S. citizens and Minneapolis residents who were protesting immigration raids.

In North Carolina, Chase Sardeson, 23, an independent and apprentice electrician in Raleigh, recalled living in Charlotte when federal agents in Operation Charlotte’s Web fanned across immigrant enclaves in tactical gear. Salvadoran restaurants shut their doors, and street vendors selling mangoes abandoned their usual posts.

“I work in construction. I’ve worked with immigrants my entire working life,” Mr. Sardeson said, explaining why immigration was one of his top election issues. “These are some of the hardest-working guys I’ve ever met. They work three jobs to support a family.”

On Tuesday, Democrats won all statewide offices in Minnesota — including closely followed races for governor, the U.S. Senate and attorney general — and majorities in both state legislative chambers. In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, flipped a Senate seat.

Heavily Hispanic counties along the border and across the country shifted dramatically back toward Democrats, particularly in Texas. In Zapata County, a South Texas border community that Mr. Trump won by 22 percentage points in 2024, James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate, won by 41 points.

The politics of immigration have changed significantly over the past decade. During Mr. Trump’s first term, more Americans tended to view the issue more favorably in a backlash against his restrictive measures and separations of families at the southwestern border.

The trend reversed sharply during the Biden administration, when illegal border crossings reached record highs and Republican governors Greg Abbott of Texas and Ron DeSantis of Florida shuttled migrants to liberal cities. By 2024, a majority of Americans, including a growing number of working-class Latinos, favored decreased immigration and stricter enforcement.

Stephanie Valencia, the president of Equis, a research group focused on understanding the Latino electorate, said Democrats were now facing a “probationary period.” The Trump administration’s dragnet had cracked open a wide lane for Democrats, she said, but the party would have to deliver on the issue and no longer avoid it.

“Both Biden and Trump got a piece of immigration wrong,” she said. “Voters have been clear on what they want: They want order, security and fairness.”

President Trump and Republicans traded blame for their losses, splitting over Mr. Trump’s tariff policies and his decision to lead the country into an unpopular war in Iran that drove up prices. But there was little reckoning over the White House approach to federal immigration enforcement and policy.

In a remarkable break from the president, Vice President JD Vance faulted the war for the Republican wipeout but went on the offensive on immigration, decrying calls for “amnesty,” a line of attack Republicans have used to halt bipartisan discussion of legislation to create and expand legal pathways for unauthorized immigrants.

“In the next few months, there’s going to be a lot of gaslighting,” he wrote in a 600-word online post. “I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement — by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.”

Across the country, many Republicans remained steadfast in their support for Mr. Trump and his mass deportation campaign, describing the border closures and deportations as a long-overdue restoration of law, order and economic fairness.

“These individuals knew the risks, they knew that what they were doing was wrong,” said Daniel Johnson, 50, a property manager in Orlando, Fla. “So, it stinks. I do feel for them. It is sad, but I mean, it’s the rules that when you break the rules, there’s consequences.”

Yet Democrats, independents and even some G.O.P. faithful saw federal overreach in what they described as indiscriminate enforcement, mistaken detentions, racial profiling and demonization of immigrants. The increase in arrests fueled anxieties not only among naturalized immigrants, but also among U.S. citizens who worried they might be perceived as being in the country unlawfully because of their appearance or accent.

Chuck Rocha, whose Latino-owned consulting firm consulted in 25 congressional races in Michigan, New York, Pennsylvania and across the Sunbelt, argued the shift on the issue did not merely happen organically.

Instead, a multimillion-dollar bilingual paid media strategy led by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries targeted Latino voters, slamming Republicans on ICE overreach, high costs and corruption. Like many analysts, Mr. Rocha drew some parallels between the Democratic breakthrough in Texas to California’s watershed fight in the 1990s over a series of anti-immigrant propositions that helped flip the state blue.

But while that moment shattered Republican viability in California, this one was more nuanced. “These voters are not wed to the Democratic Party,” he said.

The party’s messaging resonated because it reflected the grim reality in communities nationwide.

Madison Newman, 29, said fear had wracked the day care center where she worked in Kenosha, Wis.

Several Latino families had started to send their children with their passports on hand, and Latino co-workers had reported family members in suburban Milwaukee being stopped by federal immigration officials seemingly without cause, she said. “I have Mexican friends, I have Latino friends, and they’re terrified,” she said.

In Texas, tensions erupted after Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a longtime Houston construction business owner, was trailed by unmarked ICE vehicles and fatally shot on his way to work. Months later, an agent shot a Venezuelan delivery driver during a traffic stop in Austin, and in a separate incident, another ICE agent rammed another Mexican construction worker with a vehicle in Houston.

Voters in Texas and New Jersey described masked officers dragging people from cars and staking out local courthouses.

In Savannah, Ga., Felicia Murray Jackson’s older sister, Linda Davis, was killed in February, when a man being chased by immigration agents smashed into her car. For Ms. Murray Jackson, 49, a tech worker who lives to the north, in Roswell, the anger at Homeland Security officials over the tragedy propelled her toward activism.

During Atlanta’s No Kings march in October, she pleaded through a public address system, “I don’t want to hear you tell me how sorry you are for my loss. I want to hear you say I took your loss straight to the ballot box.”

For months, she knocked on doors and made phone calls to drive people to the polls. On Wednesday, as she awoke to Democratic sweeps across the country, she said she finally felt at peace.

Sean Keenan reported from Georgia. Mark Bonamo reported from New Jersey. Emily Cataneo reported from North Carolina. Valerie Boey Ramsey reported from Florida. Kim Bellware reported from Wisconsin.

item.title: ‘I Have Seen the Enemy, and It Is Us’: Inside Team Trump’s Historic Collapse
item.description:
Six days before the election, more than two dozen of President Trump’s top strategists logged onto a private video call.

The mood was grim. The discussion began with talk of cyanide.

“Do you want the white pill first, or the black pill first?” asked Tony Fabrizio, the president’s chief pollster.

Tim Saler, one of the Republican Party’s top data consultants, laid out two scenarios. In the first, the $400 million MAGA Inc. super PAC was reaching the voters that it had wanted and expected to vote. “That’s the optimistic scenario,” he said.

The other was a wipeout.

“I’m getting my affairs in order,” James Blair, who left the White House to oversee the president’s midterm strategy, said to laughter, according to four people on the call. “I suggest everybody else do the same.”

For roughly 30 minutes, the call ran on gallows humor: funeral arrangements, prison food, presidential pardons, even a brief riff on fleeing the country.

“At least Bibi won. He’ll protect us,” Mr. Blair said sarcastically of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, whose country had voted the day before. (Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc fell short of a majority, and his party soon claimed the election had been stolen.)

“Maybe we could get asylum in Israel,” Mr. Fabrizio said.

The scope of the Republican wreckage would become clear a week later.

Democrats stormed to a huge House majority and won control of the Senate, a remarkable feat powered by victories in Republican strongholds — Kansas, South Carolina, Texas — that few could have imagined a year ago.

This account of the Republican Party’s collapse is based on interviews with more than 70 people — among them lawmakers, political strategists, party leaders, pollsters, White House officials and congressional aides — who were directly involved in the midterm elections, many of whom were granted anonymity to describe private conversations and decisions.

The scale of the defeat was far from inevitable.

Republicans had record fund-raising, the world’s richest man, a favorable Supreme Court ruling on campaign finance and a demoralized, unpopular opposition.

In the Senate, they had a map that required Democrats to compete in states they hadn’t won in decades.

And in the House, the Trump team demolished the tradition of redrawing congressional lines only once a decade in order to carve up new districts to help the G.O.P. bolster its narrow majority.

What Republicans could not overcome was a president who lost the public’s trust on the economy and so much more. And what they had not counted on was an unpopular war in the Middle East — one that would close the Strait of Hormuz and push gas prices past $4 a gallon — that would rage all the way through the election.

And Democrats were ready, this time, to seize on the G.O.P. stumbles.

The slide deck that Mr. Blair had circulated over the summer to officials in the West Wing was stark.

One slide linked Republicans’ polling numbers to an Iran war timeline.

It showed how the Democratic advantage had ballooned during active hostilities, shrunk during talks over a “memorandum of understanding” and then spiked again when the cease-fire collapsed.

By the end of July, Democrats had a 10-point edge on the congressional ballot.

The “bottom line” was hard to miss. It was in highlighter yellow: Republicans could still conceivably win the House if Democrats had only a four-point edge. “But that won’t happen without an extended cease-fire, Hormuz open & gas prices falling,” the slide warned.

“A final result approaching D+10 would likely cost us the Senate.”

The results on Tuesday were even worse: Mr. Trump’s party is on track to lose the national popular congressional vote by about 13 points, according to estimates by The New York Times. It is shaping up to be the worst loss in a half-century, since the aftermath of the Watergate scandal.

Even before the polls had closed, Mr. Trump had begun to ruminate on what might have been.

“If we never went into Iran, what do you think would happen in the midterms?” the president had asked privately, according to a person who spoke to him.

What made the war such a potent force is that it told a simple story for voters.

As a candidate, Mr. Trump had promised no new wars. He started a new war.

He promised lower prices. Gas prices soared and inflation rose.

The story of the G.O.P. midterm implosion was not only a story of broken promises; it was also a story of radical overreach. After Mr. Trump came back from pariah status after Jan. 6, 2021, some advisers believed he had convinced himself that the rules of politics had been suspended for him alone. That illusion was obliterated on Tuesday night.

Over nearly two years, hubris had become the governing philosophy of Mr. Trump’s second presidency.

There was a seemingly endless string of investigative pieces revealing that Mr. Trump, his family and their close associates had used the presidency to enrich themselves brazenly. Those reports began to resonate with voters; an early October poll from Fox News showed corruption as the top voter concern. (Anna Kelly, a White House spokeswoman, said: “The President only acts in the best interest of the American people. There are no conflicts of interest.”)

In 2025, Mr. Trump began a trade war with the entire world — the pain of which was still being felt more than a year later on farms all over the suddenly competitive states of Kansas, Texas and Iowa.

Throughout it all, the president flashed indifference to the struggles of Americans that his policies had exacerbated.

Soaring gas prices? “A small price to pay,” Mr. Trump insisted.

Some members of his team grew exasperated as Mr. Trump spoke seemingly more about his new ballroom than the border, golf courses than grocery prices, interior decorations than inflation.

On the eve of the midterms, he focused his closing pitch on his refurbishment of the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall, joking that he was considering renaming it for himself rather than Abraham Lincoln.

Unlike in the past, Democrats mostly ignored the daily Trump distractions and sought to connect corruption to costs. They also told a story of a government focused on elites while average people struggled — from Jeffrey Epstein’s protected associates to the president’s $2.2 billion in personal profits.

In the House, Democrats quickly and unexpectedly countered Mr. Trump’s redistricting push and pursued strong candidates deep into red territory to spread the map. In the Senate, they found a series of blue-chip recruits who put once unthinkable states into play. In the final, frenzied weeks of the campaign, Republicans were redirecting cash from the usual swing states of North Carolina and Georgia to try to shore up traditional strongholds in South Carolina and even Mississippi.

The war in Iran, said Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader and now the speaker-in-waiting, helped “supercharge” the contrast between the two parties.

Republicans had tried to frame the midterms as a choice between “common sense and crazy,” relentlessly attacking the rising democratic socialist wing of the left.

Yet Mr. Trump’s own pollster’s final survey, taken two weeks before the election, showed that while both the MAGA Republican brand and democratic socialists were unpopular with voters, MAGA carried more baggage. When Republicans who were not planning to cast ballots were asked what it would take to earn back their vote, their top two answers were ending the war and addressing inflation.

On that final call before Election Day, Mr. Trump’s advisers were both clear-eyed and cynical about the state of the race, referring at one point to a Trump ally who ran for governor of Minnesota and demanded a recount in his primary despite losing in a landslide.

“Look, it’s fine,” Mr. Blair told the group sarcastically. “I think we’ll just pull a Mike Lindell and demand a recount regardless of how many points we’re down.”

Alex Pfeiffer, a spokesman for the MAGA Inc. super PAC, said that the group’s “sober and clear-eyed view of the political environment,” led to investing in House races Republicans are leading in, in Maine, Florida, Tennessee, New York and Texas.

“The people peddling these made up quotes and false gossip not only demean and belittle the historic and generous investment by the president into the party’s midterm effort, but they also slander the hard work of the many who contributed to this effort,” he said in a statement. “They are cowards and losers.”

A White House official, who declined to speak on the record, said in response to the reporting for this article: “President Trump was not on the ballot, and it’s proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot. Candidate quality matters, and President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves.”

The official repeated that the president, who acknowledged earlier on Wednesday that the war affected the midterms, had over and over again said Iran can’t procure a nuclear weapon.

While Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, painstakingly recruited top-tier Senate candidates, Mr. Trump took a series of steps that endangered the Republican majority.

After Senator Joni Ernst of Iowa flirted with opposing Mr. Trump’s most controversial nominees and Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina voted against his signature tax-and-spending bill, Mr. Trump’s allies threatened to end their careers. Both decided to retire, creating vulnerable open seats that had been held by Republicans.

In North Carolina, Mr. Trump cleared the field for Michael Whatley, a former lobbyist and Republican National Committee chairman, who proved a lackluster candidate and lost to Roy Cooper, the state’s popular Democratic former governor.

After Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina died in July, Mr. Trump supported tapping his sister, Darline, to not just replace him temporarily but also to run for a full six-year term. In doing so, he elevated an inexperienced candidate with no fund-raising base, and she went on to lose in a state that had not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998.

But no candidate proved more costly to the party than Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden Texas attorney general. Mr. Trump endorsed him over Senator John Cornyn, the Republican incumbent, ignoring a year of warnings that Mr. Paxton would put the seat in jeopardy. Republicans were ultimately forced to spend close to $300 million in Texas — money that could have gone to shore up candidates in other states. Mr. Paxton lost by 12 points.

On another recent call, the Trump team mocked the haplessness of some of the Republicans they were trying to elect.

“I have seen the enemy,” Mr. Blair told the group a week earlier. “And it is us.”

Mr. Fabrizio replied: “In many places.”

In May 2025, Mr. Schumer arrived at Wildflower Farms, an upscale resort in New York’s Hudson Valley, for a secretive retreat with donors and party officials. He desperately needed to expand the Senate map.

To win control of the Senate, Democrats needed to hold all of their seats and flip at least four, including in states that Mr. Trump won handily in 2024.

Mr. Schumer spent months wooing Mr. Cooper and took at least three trips to Ohio to coax former Senator Sherrod Brown, who had lost in 2024 but had a populist brand that matched the country’s mood.

“If you retire and we lose the majority by one vote, you won’t enjoy your retirement,” Mr. Schumer recalled telling Mr. Brown, 73.

Both ran and won.

In the House, where Democrats had fallen three seats short in 2024, recruiters went hunting in districts Mr. Trump had carried by 10 points or more, betting early that the emboldened president would overreach.

An election post-mortem by the Democratic House Majority PAC circulated in April 2025 found two factors stood out among the party’s stronger 2024 candidates: being “perceived as moderate” and focusing on the economy.

“If we wanted to compete deeper in red districts, we needed to find candidates who are not immediately off-putting,” said Mike Smith, the PAC’s president.

They set about recruiting candidates with distinctive biographies: military veterans, doctors, farmers, a smokejumper, a Tejano music star — just about anyone who didn’t scream professional politician.

Mr. Trump, meanwhile, was trying to redraw the House battlefield itself.

In the spring of 2025, Mr. Blair, then his deputy chief of staff, brought the president a plan to redraw congressional maps mid-decade to make seats safer for Republicans. The gerrymandering push started in Texas and soon spread to other Republican-led states.

When Mr. Jeffries first heard about the Texas gambit, he turned to his advisers in disbelief and declared, “You’ve got to be fucking kidding me.” He flew to Texas to urge state legislators to take a stand, and many Democrats fled the state to slow down the legislative process.

But the Trump-inspired play went through and Republicans carved themselves out five new seats that Mr. Trump would have carried by double digits in 2024 — seemingly enough to withstand even a dip in support in the midterms.

Democrats fought back. California voters approved Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to create five new seats favoring Democrats, and Virginia voters approved a map creating another four, though the Supreme Court later struck it down.

From the start, Mr. Blair was cocksure about his redistricting plan, and he and the president dismissed Republicans who worried about the maneuver backfiring.

But by April 2026, Democrats had good reason to believe that they had neutralized the threat by redrawing districts in several blue states. Mr. Jeffries held a celebratory news conference featuring a poster with the faces of Mr. Trump and Mr. Blair and an anonymous quote that had appeared in an article about redistricting in The Times: “Maximum warfare everywhere all the time.”

When Mr. Blair saw the poster, he texted one of Mr. Jeffries’s top aides, Gideon Bragin: “Can you send a copy of this to my office?”

Instead, it remained inside House Democratic headquarters through Election Day, when a blue tidal wave washed over even many of the districts drawn to favor Republicans.

As 2026 began, the administration’s immigration enforcement surge turned violent in Minneapolis when two protesters were shot and killed by federal agents. Both killings were captured on video.

Mr. Trump told advisers he didn’t like how the videos looked.

Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, had spent months privately trying to steer him away from the hard-line immigration approach favored by Stephen Miller, the president’s top policy adviser.

Soon after Minneapolis, Democrats’ internal polls showed the party taking the edge on immigration for the first time. What had been one of Mr. Trump’s perennial strengths was for a period his top liability, according to one of the president’s senior strategists.

Then, about five weeks after the second shooting, Mr. Trump took the country to war in Iran.

Mr. Blair at first shared his boss’s optimism that the war would be a quick success. He reassured skeptical colleagues that the conflict would not be the political disaster some feared because some Defense Department officials had assured the White House it would be resolved rapidly.

But the president’s four-to-six-week timeline stretched into months.

In public, Mr. Trump crowed about a decisive military triumph. In private, advisers briefed him on the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, spiking prices of gas and fertilizer and an alarming depletion of American weaponry.

Mr. Fabrizio’s focus groups in March, about two weeks into the conflict, showed that voters did not understand why the president had started the war. They saw a broken promise that was making life more expensive.

Former allies on the antiwar right, including Tucker Carlson and the former Georgia congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, were now in open rebellion.

Mr. Trump knew the war was draining his support, according to advisers, but for a brief moment it seemed that he had found himself a way out of the mess. By mid-June, Vice President JD Vance had negotiated a memorandum of understanding with Iran, and the Trump political team exhaled. Mr. Fabrizio’s first poll of the proposal found that voters aware of the deal favored it by 41 percentage points, and 67 percent thought it would bring down gas prices.

But G.O.P. Iran hawks, including Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, pressed Mr. Trump to keep the pressure on Tehran. The deal fell apart and the war dragged on.

Mr. Trump never stopped raising money after the 2024 election, assembling a roughly $400 million war chest that he made clear to advisers he saw as “my money.”

By August, with the election less than 100 days away, Republican Senate strategists still had no clarity on where Team Trump would spend. One described being “shocked at how ill-prepared they were.”

A Trump adviser said a plan existed but could not be shared because the president had not approved it.

Some days, Mr. Trump told advisers privately: “We’ve gotta win. Anything we gotta do.” On others, he sounded as if he couldn’t care less. “It says something very nice about me that they just can’t win without me,” he told aides.

Mr. Blair and others had to make the case to the president to sign off on the spending. Mr. Trump withheld his approval until the end of the summer.

The delay was costly: Ad prices soar as elections near.

One week in mid-October on a single station in Anchorage, the Trump super PAC paid nearly four times as much money as the leading Democratic super PAC did to air roughly 70 percent fewer commercials because it had not reserved the time well in advance.

The Democratic group paid $2,700 for a commercial on the local evening news; Mr. Trump’s super PAC paid $30,000 for the same slot.

Typically, endangered lawmakers distance themselves from an unpopular president in midterm elections. Team Trump wanted to do the opposite.

“We have taken that old construct and flipped it on its head,” said Chris LaCivita, the co-manager of Mr. Trump’s 2024 campaign.

Thus, the first modern midterm convention was born, a two-day celebration of the president in Dallas in September that few members of his party had wanted.

During his convention speech, Mr. Trump rolled out a splashy new proposal to send $5,000 to every American adult — but only if Republicans won.

Almost no one knew it was coming, including his senior political advisers, the speaker and the Senate majority leader.

The idea had not even been polled before Mr. Trump said it. And when a similar proposal was tested, Mr. Trump’s team found it did little to move voters toward Republicans. Some of the president’s own advisers cringed at the giveaway, with one describing it as a naked effort to “bribe” people for their votes.

The convention did bring one piece of good news: money. On the first day, Elon Musk sent $75 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC led by allies of the Senate majority leader, John Thune of South Dakota. It was one of the largest single contributions in American history.

At the convention, Mr. Paxton made his way into the fund’s suite, where Alex Latcham, the super PAC’s executive director, made a somewhat cryptic remark to him.

“You’re going to be happy tomorrow.”

The ads were about to begin.

Mr. Musk would spend more than $450 million to aid Republicans in the midterms, much of it in Texas to try to save Mr. Paxton. The super PAC he funded spent tens of millions on ads attacking the Democratic nominee, James Talarico, for his support of transgender rights, mirroring a line of attack that the Trump team had used effectively in 2024.

In other races, the focus on transgender ads became a point of disagreement between officials at the Senate Leadership Fund and Mr. Trump’s operation, which argued that the 2026 election was fundamentally about the economy and that running ads on other topics would be less effective. Senate G.O.P. strategists saw economic messages falling flat in the current political environment in some states.

The fight to save the Senate was hampered by party leadership that could barely work together. Mr. Trump and Senate G.O.P. leaders, Mr. Thune among them, never grew close. The president endorsed Mr. Paxton over their objections. And when Trump advisers met with officials from the top Republican super PAC at Camp David in March 2026 to plan for the midterms, no one from the National Republican Senatorial Committee was invited.

In late August, Julie Merz, the top strategist at the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, gathered her team and pulled up a slide estimating a 35 percent chance of a “blue wave.”

“It’s our job,” she recalled saying, “to hand out as many surfboards as possible.”

Committee officials made the party’s most vulnerable incumbents an unusual offer: Instead of spending millions defending them, the party would move the money into deeper red territory and poll their seats to see if they needed the resources back. Most agreed, freeing up around $10 million to expand the map.

Not long after the Republican convention in Dallas, diesel prices hit all-time highs.

In the Senate, it got so bad for the G.O.P. that by early October Republicans were ordering up polls in seemingly unthinkable states, like South Dakota and Idaho.

A month before the election, the Senate Leadership Fund pulled ads from North Carolina, ceding the state to redirect money to Kansas, then South Carolina and eventually Mississippi — a state Mr. Trump had carried by nearly 23 points two years ago.

“Battleground Mississippi,” Mr. Trump’s advisers called it mockingly on a call.

In the House, the deterioration was perhaps worse.

At one point, top officials with the Congressional Leadership Fund and Mr. Trump’s super PACs had decided to give up trying to flip Representative Henry Cuellar’s South Texas seat — only to realize that Speaker Mike Johnson was set to be in the district the day the ads were going to come off the air. They delayed the announcement for a day to spare Mr. Johnson an embarrassing episode.

Mr. Cuellar won re-election in a landslide.

In the end, the map shifted so far left that House Republicans — who polled more than 100 seats — could not keep up. It surprised even some leading Democrats.

At a September dinner, Rahm Emanuel, who ran the House Democrats’ campaign arm in the 2006 wave, asked the party’s top recruits how much Mr. Trump had won their districts by. When Zach Dembo, a military veteran and former federal prosecutor running in Kentucky’s Sixth District, said 15 points, Mr. Emanuel looked at him in disbelief.

Mr. Dembo won.

The last Sunday before Election Day, Mr. Jeffries arranged for a symbolic final stop to a battleground district.

He went to Alabama, where Republicans had redrawn Representative Shomari Figures’s district to favor their party after a Supreme Court decision weakened the Voting Rights Act. It was important to go there, Mr. Jeffries said, because “he was facing a renewed effort to subject the African American community to Jim Crow-like tactics.”

“It’s fair to say that Shomari and I both felt the weight of history given the fact that the civil rights movement led by Dr. King, Rosa Parks, and so many others began in the very place where we were ending this all important 2026 campaign,” Mr. Jeffries said.

Mr. Figures won his race on Tuesday.

On the way to the airport, Mr. Jeffries made an unpublicized stop at the Freedom Monument Sculpture Park that remembers the history of enslaved people in America.

In January, Mr. Jeffries is now set to become the first Black speaker in American history.
